rules.on_page: In all 28 'partly' verdicts the crop stopped short of the passage's end because the locator's end match was weak. The part shown was printed on the page in every case, so 'partly' counts as on the page, for the part checked.
rules.one_item: Yes when every printing carries the item the story's title names, even if some printings' matched text runs a little into the next paragraph. No when the shared text is a run of separate items (a digest), or when the story chains items so that some printings do not carry the titled item. Reports of one legislature's sittings printed as one continuing report count as one item.
rules.transcription: Fact-changing (major): a number, date or proper name read as a different plausible one; a word read as a different real word that changes the sense; words, a line, a signature or table data dropped or added. Minor: garbles a reader would recognise as errors, spelling or word-form variants, near-synonyms that keep the sense, silent corrections of printed misprints, and dropped or added small words that do not change the sense.

for_the_owner.London, 1770: a paragraph on what 'appea: A one-sentence London paragraph that turns on private lives: what 'appeared upon a late trial' about a nobleman's mistresses since his marriage (R-04); it names no one. Printed by every paper that survives for its weeks (the Massachusetts Spy, the New-Hampshire Gazette, which prints 'seven' where the others have 'eleven', and both Virginia Gazettes): it would be admitted by the rule's first part if the owner sees it as a public matter. In 4 of the 4 papers that survive for its weeks (needs 4).

for_user_decision.A paragraph on a nobleman's private life: As built (R-04): a one-sentence London paragraph on what 'appeared upon a late trial' about a nobleman's mistresses since his marriage is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks, but it turns on private lives, so it is listed for the owner, without names (it names no one). If the owner sees it as a public matter, it is admitted by the rule's first part.
for_user_decision.The floor of four papers before 23 Augus: As built: before 23 August only three papers survive (in January and February fewer), so no item printed only then reaches the bar of 4; the town of Boston's account of the night of 5 March 1770, and its committee to the Lieutenant Governor, are printed by all three papers that survive for their weeks and are below the bar, as is the King's speech of 9 January. All three admitted items were first printed in October.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1770 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 32 items printed somewhere; the collection begins in 1770, so there are no families of 1769). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1770 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (21 texts). For every text at the bar or one paper short of it, the papers the comparison missed were looked for again on their pages (the best page within the text's weeks) and read. A sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers, over every page, found items the families miss (as X-1803-09); each was read. Every admitted item was then counted by phrase searches of its opening over all 448 pages in both transcriptions, and every hit read (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).

value.paper_counting: 1770 has 4 catalogue series, which are 4 papers: the New-Hampshire Gazette and Historical Chronicle (Portsmouth; 50 issues) all year; two Virginia Gazettes, both printed at Williamsburg by different printers, Alexander Purdie and John Dixon (sn84024739; 26 issues, from 15 February) and William Rind (sn84024741; 19 issues, from 25 January); and the Massachusetts Spy (Boston; 17 issues) from 23 August. Papers in print in any three weeks: 1 to 3 before late August; 4 in most windows from late August to December.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; digests are not admitted. 1770 has four papers, so an item reaches the bar only when all four print it: every eligible item is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks, three are admitted, and one that turns on private lives is listed for the owner (R-04); nothing is chosen. The fourth paper, the Massachusetts Spy, survives from 23 August, so no item reaches the bar unless it was still being printed after that day.

counted_item_by_item.A letter and a paragraph on it: Three papers print an extract of a private letter from Constantinople ('The north east parts of Europe are at present both delighted and terrified ...'); the Massachusetts Spy prints, earlier and under another London date, a two-sentence paragraph of its own on what the letter says ('A LETTER from Constantinople says, That the Grand Seignor has at last taken the field in person ...'). As built, the paragraph recites part of the letter and is not counted as a printing of it (C-07), so the letter is in 3 of 4; counted as another printed form (C-02) it would be in 4 of 4 and admitted (for_user_decision).
counted_item_by_item.A notice quoted in other papers' words: The Commissary's notice to the clergy of Virginia of a convention on an American episcopate is printed whole by the two Virginia Gazettes; the Massachusetts Spy and the New-Hampshire Gazette print a paragraph of their own that quotes its passage on the episcopate, which is not a printing of the notice (C-06, C-07), so the notice is in 2 of 4.
counted_item_by_item.A page without a RevX transcription: The Massachusetts Spy of 9 May prints Mr. Wilkes's letter to Sir Fletcher Norton on a page that has no RevX transcription; the comparison by the opening missed it, and the look for the missing paper found it in the page's CA text, so the letter is in 4 of 4 and admitted; its excerpt there comes from the CA text.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: The admitted item was counted by phrase searches of its own words, every hit read; its papers are in the README's table of stories. The texts read and below the bar are listed in not_admitted with their counts.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs in runs of news: London news of the printers' case and the City's quarrel with the House of Commons (March to May 1771) reached the papers in runs of paragraphs and documents, each counted by its own opening (C-09): Mr. Wilkes's letter to the Speaker is printed by all four papers; the Guildhall Rota Book, the counsel's opinion, the case put to counsel, the Lord Mayor's habeas corpus and Lord Chatham's speech and motion are each in 3 of 4.
counted_item_by_item.Shared phrases that are not one item: Of the 15 clusters the sweep found in 4 papers, 6 are passages of Mr. Wilkes's letter, 1 is the Constantinople letter with the Spy's paragraph, 1 is the episcopate notice, and 7 are set phrases shared by different texts: the opening of addresses to governors ('May it please your Excellency, WE his Majesty's'), governors' titles, 'one of his Majesty's Justices of the Peace', an advertisers' formula, 'one of His Majesty's Principal Secretaries of State', 'at the Secretary of State's Office, in Cleveland Row' and 'the Lord Mayor and Mr. Alderman Oliver to the'. Two of the paragraphs under those phrases, a London report of the King of Spain's order for restoring Port Egmont and one that the City would meet on Tower-hill when Parliament was prorogued, were counted by their own words: each is in 3 of 4.

for_user_decision.The floor of four papers where three sur: As built: four papers survive only in January, from late April to May and in parts of June and July; in the rest of the year two or three survive, so nothing printed only then reaches the bar of 4, as in 1770, 1772, 1789 and 1790. 1771 has one story, printed in May.
for_user_decision.The letter from Constantinople and the S: As built: the Massachusetts Spy's two-sentence paragraph on what a letter from Constantinople says (under London, 3 November 1770) recites part of the letter and is not counted as a printing of it (C-07), so the extract of the letter is in 3 of the 4 papers of its weeks and below the bar. If the owner counts the paragraph as another printed form of the letter (C-02, as the Hamburg letter printed in other words in 1772), the letter is in 4 of 4 and is admitted by the rule's first part, after a scan check of its printings: 1771 would have 2 stories.

value.paper_counting: 1771 has 4 catalogue series, which are 4 papers: the Massachusetts Spy (Boston; 25 issues, none from 2 February to 8 May or from 1 November to 18 December; a 26th filed under 1771 is the issue of 27 December 1770), the New-Hampshire Gazette and Historical Chronicle (Portsmouth; 50 issues, from 18 January), and two Virginia Gazettes, both printed at Williamsburg by different printers, Alexander Purdie and John Dixon (sn84024739; 48 issues) and William Rind (sn84024741; 12 issues, the last of 18 July). Papers in print in any three weeks: 4 in January, from late April to May and in parts of June and July; 3 or 2 in the rest of the year.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; digests are not admitted. Single paragraphs from runs of news are counted by their own words (C-09). In 1771 four papers survive only in January, from late April to May and in parts of June and July, when the Massachusetts Spy and Rind's Virginia Gazette both have issues: 1 item is printed by all four papers and admitted.

counted_item_by_item.Accounts of one hurricane: The papers printed several accounts of the hurricane of late August in the Leeward Islands, each counted by its own words: from Christiansted (chosen, 4 of 5), Antigua (3 of 5), Basseterre (3 of 4) and others in fewer papers.
counted_item_by_item.One letter in two wordings: Rind's Virginia Gazette prints the letter from Hamburg of 25 August on the revolution in Sweden in other words ('A letter from Hambourg, dated August 25, says ... two couriers, dispatched from Stockholm ...'); it is counted with the other three (C-02).
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: The 13 admitted and chosen items and the 4 listed for the owner were counted by phrase searches of their openings, every hit read; their papers are in the README's table of stories. The texts read and below the bar are listed in not_admitted with their counts.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs in runs of news: London, Boston and Philadelphia news reached the papers in runs of short paragraphs, and the four papers often reprinted the same runs. value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1772 that reach 3 or more papers, and those of 1771 over the 1772 pages, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 135 items printed somewhere, 5 reaching 4 papers by the finder's counts; items_from_1771.json). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1772 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (92 texts). For every text one paper short of the bar, the missing paper was looked for again on its pages, by the text's words (the best page within its weeks) and by its names (the pages holding three or more of its proper names), and read. A sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers, over every page, found items the families miss (as X-1803-09): 55 clusters, each read, among them single paragraphs from runs of news printed by every surviving paper. Every admitted, chosen and listed item was then counted by phrase searches of its opening over all 675 pages in both transcriptions, and every hit read (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).

value.paper_counting: 1772 has 6 catalogue series, which are 5 papers: the Massachusetts Spy (Boston; 48 issues) all year, under two catalogue numbers (sn83021193 to 1 October; sn83021194, 'or, Thomas's Boston Journal', from 8 October), counted as one paper (C-04); the New-Hampshire Gazette and Historical Chronicle (Portsmouth; 52 issues); two Virginia Gazettes, both printed at Williamsburg by different printers, Alexander Purdie and John Dixon (sn84024739; 52 issues) and William Rind (sn84024741; 18 issues, from 6 February: five in February to May, the rest from 8 October); and one issue of the South-Carolina and American General Gazette (Charlestown, 5 October). Papers in print in any three weeks: 3 (June to mid-September, and a few weeks in January, March and April) or 4; 5 in the weeks of 5 October.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; digests are not admitted. Single paragraphs from runs of news are counted by their own words (C-09). In 1772 four papers survive only where Rind's Virginia Gazette has an issue (late January to May, and October to December), and five in the weeks of the South-Carolina and American General Gazette's one issue (5 October): 12 items are printed by every surviving paper and admitted, 1 eligible item printed by four of five papers is chosen, and 4 that turn on private persons are listed for the owner (R-04).

chosen.New York, 2 December 1773: 'Letters were: chosen: the only eligible New York report of December on the East India Company's tea, so December has a story; printed by 4 of the 5 papers of its weeks (the Massachusetts Spy has no printing)

counted_item_by_item.A document under two introductions: The South Carolina Commons House's resolutions answering Virginia's are printed under a Charlestown report of 13 July by three papers and under another Charlestown report, of 16 July, by Rind's Virginia Gazette; they are counted together (C-02, as 1793's list of the powers under two introductions).
counted_item_by_item.One report in two wordings: Some reports reached the papers in two wordings, which are counted together as one item (C-02, as the Hamburg letter of 1772): Captain Henshaw's news from St. Vincent (a New York paragraph of 4 February and a Philadelphia one of 8 February), the letter from Annapolis, Sir Jeffery Amherst's swearing in, the Hotel Dieu, the emigration from the north of Ireland, the King's gifts at Portsmouth, Captain Eve's report from the Bay of Honduras, the King of Prussia and Hanover, and the armaments of the Emperor and the King of Prussia; the Massachusetts Spy prints the London paragraph on the Sheriffs of Middlesex's letter without its first sentence. Another account of the same event, in other words and with other facts, is another text: the New-Hampshire Gazette's account of the Lord Mayor's election in October is not counted with the London paragraph the others print.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that are not printings: The phrase searches also hit pages that only quote an item or print another text in its words (C-07): the two Houses' addresses answering the King's speech of 26 November 1772 and a paragraph quoting it; other assemblies' resolutions answering Virginia's of 12 March; later paragraphs on the Orphan House in Georgia; letters from Paris on the fire at the Hotel Dieu; a later paragraph on Lord William Campbell's patent; the Governor's message on the letters laid before the Massachusetts House. They are not counted.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: The 49 admitted and chosen items, the 29 eligible items not chosen, the 3 for the owner and the 20 read below the bar were counted by phrase searches of their own words, every hit read; their papers are in counted_items.json.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs in runs of news: London, Boston, New York and Philadelphia news reached the papers in runs of short paragraphs, which the four papers reprinted in different orders and weeks apart. Each paragraph is counted by its own opening sentence (C-09): 34 of the 48 admitted items are single paragraphs or letters from such runs.
counted_item_by_item.Repeated printings and a misfiled issue: The Custom-House notice of 15 December 1772 was printed three times by each paper; all twelve printings are in the ledger (as 1779 and 1782 keep repeated printings). Purdie and Dixon's Virginia Gazette of 11 March has its RevX transcriptions filed one page off (in the release's revx_page_map); the notice on its page 4 is cut from the CA text.

The other thin years reviewed have 1 to 30 stories, and a standard year about 20 to 35; Y-THIN's 'reopen if' names this case (the bar admitting far more than the standard years). value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1773 that reach 3 or more papers, and those of 1772 over the 1773 pages, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 274 items printed somewhere, 38 reaching 4 papers by the finder's counts; items_from_1772.json: 9). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1773 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (189 texts, 31 at the bar by that count). For every text one paper short of the bar (132), the missing paper was looked for again on its pages, by the text's words (the best page within its weeks) and by its names (the pages holding three or more of its proper names, ranked by the share of the opening's words they hold), and the pages found were read. value.paper_counting: 1773 has 6 catalogue series, which are 6 papers: the Massachusetts Spy, or Thomas's Boston Journal (Boston; 40 issues, none between 16 April and 6 May, 17 June and 22 July, or 26 November and 16 December), the New-Hampshire Gazette and Historical Chronicle (Portsmouth; 53 issues), the two Virginia Gazettes printed at Williamsburg by Alexander Purdie and John Dixon (sn84024739; 52 issues) and by William Rind (sn84024741; 52 issues), Dunlap's Pennsylvania Packet (Philadelphia; 10 issues, from 25 October) and the Connecticut Courant (Hartford; one issue, 28 December). Papers in print in any three weeks: 4 in most of the year; 3 for items first printed from 18 June to 1 July; 5 from early October; 6 from 8 to 27 December.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; digests are not admitted. Single paragraphs from runs of news are counted by their own words (C-09). In 1773 four papers survive in most weeks, so an item printed by all four is admitted: 48 items are admitted by the rule's first part, from January to November; 1 eligible item printed by four of the five papers of its weeks is chosen for December, a month the admitted items do not reach.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1774 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 692 items found on the pages, 259 in 4 or more papers by the finder's count), and again with the families of 1773 over the 1774 pages (items_from_1773.json: 23 items, none in 4 or more). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page and counted again by its opening; a sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers found 2,025 passages in 775 runs, and the runs no finder item covers were read (184 at first; after a fault in the first coverage check was fixed on 24 November, 122 runs are uncovered, all read). value.paper_counting: 1774 has 8 catalogue series, which are 7 papers (C-04): the Connecticut Courant is sn82016376 to 24 May and sn82016139 (The Connecticut Courant and Hartford Weekly Intelligencer) from 7 June. Five papers run all year; Rind's Virginia Gazette survives for 13 January and from 21 April; the Pennsylvania Journal for 27 July only. 5 to 7 papers are in print in any three weeks. No 1774 issue has a corrected date; the release's map lists 5 misfiled RevX pages, on which no admitted printing stands. The Courant to 31 May is dated by weeks and filed under the first date (X-1774-12).
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN, as amended on 23 November 2026, the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; as in R-01, the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35); one affair's items as in X-1800-01; digests are not admitted; sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) as in every year. In 1774 5 to 7 papers survive for any item's weeks, so the bar is 4 papers for every item.

counted_item_by_item.Below every surviving paper by their own: The London report of the merchants' meeting of 4 January, the London paragraph on Spain's assurances and the report of the Dutch fleet are each in 5 papers by their own words (the count's sixth paper prints another text); General Washington's orders of 4 July are in 5. They are listed as not chosen.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Of 441 eligible items, 45 reach every paper that survives for their weeks by the count; read again by their own words, 28 do (one of them, a curiosity about a private person, is listed for the owner), and 27 are admitted. 9 are chosen, among them the Congress's declaration of 6 July (5 papers by its own words); the others are listed as not chosen.
counted_item_by_item.The Congress's two petitions: The petition of October 1774 and the petition of 8 July 1775 open with the same words; each is counted by its own text and pages.
counted_item_by_item.The King's proclamation for suppressing: Counted with Purdie's report of it in indirect speech (C-02): 5 papers of 7.
counted_item_by_item.The London letter of 31 May: Counted with the Philadelphia letter of 29 July that quotes it (C-02): 6 papers.
counted_item_by_item.The Lords' protest: Counted with the reported form in Purdie's Virginia Gazette ('That they cannot agree to commit themselves'), a paragraph made from it (C-02).
counted_item_by_item.The battle of 17 June: The express account ('By an Express which arrived here on Saturday evening') is in 3 papers by its own words; the Providence letter (4) is chosen.

for_user_decision.Printed forms counted together: As built (X-1775-04): the Lords' protest with its reported form, the London letter of 31 May with the Philadelphia letter quoting it, the King's proclamation with Purdie's report of it (C-02).

for_user_decision.The choice for 1775: As built (X-1775-01): 27 groups admitted by the rule's first part and 9 chosen, 24 stories and 206 printings; the other eligible items are listed as not chosen.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1775 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 838 items found on the pages, 354 in 4 or more papers by the finder's count), and again with the families of 1774 over the 1775 pages (items_from_1774.json: 77 items, 8 in 4 or more). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page and counted again by its opening; a sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers found 895 runs, and the runs no finder item covers were read. Counted item by item (452 entries), 441 items meet the bar (count_1775.md). The items printed by every paper that survives for their weeks by the count were counted again by their own words with phrase searches over all 1,286 pages in both transcriptions; the admitted and chosen items were read on every page.

value.paper_counting: 1775 has 7 catalogue series, which are 7 papers: the Connecticut Courant, Dunlap's Pennsylvania Packet, Gaine's New-York Gazette and Dixon and Hunter's Virginia Gazette run all year; the New-Hampshire Gazette survives in 39 issues, to 12 December; Purdie's Virginia Gazette from its first issue, 3 February; the Pennsylvania Journal for 27 December only. No 1775 issue has a corrected date; the release's map lists 2 misfiled RevX pages, on which no admitted printing stands.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN, as amended on 23 November 2026, the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; as in R-01, the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35); one affair's items as in X-1800-01; digests are not admitted; sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) as in every year. In 1775 5 to 7 papers survive for any item's weeks (6 for most of the year), so the bar is 4 papers for every item.

value.method: Round three of 1776. On 11 November 2026 the owner set the rule 'every story alike': a reviewed story is described by what kind of text it is and whose account, in the papers' own words, never as what happened; sensitive subjects get no special treatment. Items that earlier rounds held back for framing are therefore counted by the year's own rule, exactly like any other item: what reaches it is admitted, what does not stays out. As before, an excerpt ends before the names of private people where it can, and stories that turn on private people stay out. Rounds one and two left out the reports of Cherokee and Creek plans, each counted by the item finder in 8 papers. Both were read again with phrase searches over all 2,319 pages of 1776 in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns_round3.json, phrase_hits_round3.json), every hit was read, the papers in print in their weeks without a hit were searched with loose keywords (no missed printing), and every printing was checked against its page scan by AI reviewers (scan_batches/batch_16.json and batch_17.json, SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points_round3.json).

The separate letters of a correspondence are counted one by one (the exchange of prisoners; General Gates and General Burgoyne).
counted_item_by_item.Not items of their own: Congress's order of 16 June to publish the letters on the exchange of prisoners (the heading of that publication); a sentence on the King of Prussia's ports inside different letters; the last sentence of the Albany letter of 11 August, which two papers print as a paragraph of its own.
counted_item_by_item.Pages first counted for another text: Read and taken out: two pages with Congress's thanks to Colonel Greene (not the thanks to Lieutenant Colonels Meigs and Barton); two pages with an answer headed 'To John Burgoyne' (not General Burgoyne's proclamation); the Pennsylvania Packet's page of the messages that passed before the convention of Saratoga; a page with a different letter from Moses Creek of the same date.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that reword, summarise or recite a: Not counted (C-07): Purdie's summary of the April letters on the exchange of prisoners; Dixon and Hunter's paraphrase of General Washington's proclamation of 25 January; a Baltimore paragraph about Governor Henry's proclamation; the state proclamations that recite Congress's resolution for a thanksgiving; a Loan Office notice in Purdie's Virginia Gazette (10 and 31 October, 14 November) that restates Congress's resolution of 10 September on the interest of loan office certificates.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted item by item over all 1,320 pages, 91 items met the bar in the count of 23 November. The reading and the phrase searches left 88 eligible items (86 groups, and two reports of an affair already chosen), and the sweep checked again on 24 November added 9 (X-1777-08), 97 in all: three items fell below the bar by their own words (the brig Warren, the London paragraph on the high treason bill, Captain Fisk's prize), one letter is merged with the letter it sends, and Sir Joseph Yorke's memorial reaches the bar with its two translations counted together. One item is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks and is admitted: the articles of convention of Saratoga (7 of 7). Of the others, 35 are chosen (26 stories, 36 groups, 186 printings), 60 are listed as eligible and not chosen, and one that turns on a private person is listed for the owner.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: C-02: the Baltimore report of a French fleet at Charleston in two forms (3 + 2 papers), Sir Joseph Yorke's memorial in two translations (2 + 2) and the Philadelphia paragraph on prisoners and deserters after the landing at Elk in two forms (3 + 1). Each reaches the bar only together (Q-04).
counted_item_by_item.The bar: Y-THIN: more than half of the papers that survive for the item's weeks (a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and at least 4. 1777 has 10 papers; 5 to 9 are in print in an item's weeks, so the bar is 4 for most items and 5 where the weeks reach late April to early June, when the two Charleston papers survive.

for_user_decision.Choosing among the eligible items (X-177: As built: as X-1800-01 and the standard years' chosen band, the most widely printed items of each month and kind are chosen; of an affair in the same weeks, the most widely printed item, with the separate public acts printed as widely beside it (a letter and its answer, a speech and the address to it, the convention and the letter on it). Not chosen as items of an affair already chosen: General Washington's letter of 20 June, General Schuyler's letter of 7 July, General St. Clair's letter to the printer on General Schuyler, a letter from headquarters on the papers' 'prejudice' toward General St. Clair, General Washington's letter to Congress of 16 July, the Baltimore paragraph on the Eastern Shore rising and the Providence account of General Prescott's capture. Every month from January to November has a story; no eligible item was first printed in December.
for_user_decision.Names in the letters from Moses Creek an: As built (C-12): the letter of 26 July from Moses Creek tells of a skirmish at Fort Edward and of a young woman taken from a house and killed; the excerpts end before her name and the description does not give it. Her death was much reported in 1777; the owner may prefer her name shown, as the papers print it. The letter from Pittsburgh of 24 March names the man who returned from the Indian country with the news; the excerpts keep his name, as shipmasters named as sources of news are kept (C-12), and end before the names of settlers killed; the owner may prefer his name cut.

for_user_decision.Paragraphs of runs of news, a notice and: As built: single paragraphs of runs of London and foreign news are eligible as items (C-09); one is chosen (London, 17 February, on the preparations for the campaign, the only eligible item first printed in May), the eight others are not. for_user_decision.The papers in print and the bar (X-1777-: As built: Y-THIN as amended (B1), with 10 papers (11 catalogue series) and 5 to 9 papers in print in an item's weeks; the bar (4 for most items, 5 where the weeks reach late April to early June) makes 97 items eligible. value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1777 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 341 items printed somewhere), and the families of 1776 were looked for on the 1777 pages (items_from_1776.json: 39 items). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page (about 220 words of its text, both transcriptions); every page was swept for seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers; every candidate was counted by its own opening over all 1,320 pages in both transcriptions and the matches were read; every admitted story and every candidate set aside was searched with phrase searches (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).

value.paper_counting: 1777 has 11 catalogue series, which are 10 papers: Dunlap's Pennsylvania Packet (Philadelphia, to 9 September) and The Pennsylvania Packet (Lancaster, from 29 November) are one paper (C-04). The Newport Gazette and the New-York Gazette were printed in towns the British held. The release's map lists two misfiled RevX pages for 1777 (the Freeman's Journal of 8 March, pages 2 and 3); no 1777 issue has a corrected date.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (register Y-THIN) as amended by the owner's choice B1 on 23 November 2026: an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4; digests are not. As in R-01, items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35, a target, not a quota); one affair's items as in X-1800-01. The eligible items not chosen are listed with their counts and are not checked against the scans. Sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) apply as in every year.

counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains documents printed together or sharing formulas: the two draught bills and the commissioners' later papers through the bills' titles; the commissioners' declarations and requisition of 26 August through their titles; the lists of the thirteen states; standing notices of the New-York Gazette. Each text was counted by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted by their own words, 76 items of 1778 are eligible (more than half of the papers that survive for their weeks, and at least 4): 55 in 4 papers, 18 in 5, 3 in 6, none in 7. Three are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks and are admitted (the landing at Bedford, 4 of 4; Congress's resolution of 4 September, 5 of 5; the manifesto of Congress, 6 of 6). 30 more are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; the 33 items make 26 stories (21 single items and 5 parents holding the other 12 as sub-stories). 42 eligible items are not chosen; one turns on private persons and waits for the owner. 51 more candidates were counted and are below the bar.

for_the_owner.A general court martial at Lancaster, Ma: Eligible (4 of the 6 papers that survive for its weeks), March and April. It turns on two persons tried as spies, one of them a private inhabitant, and reports their sentence; by R-04 it is not admitted without the owner's decision, and public files describe it without names.

for_user_decision.Pages filed under other dates (X-1778-07: As built: the Freeman's Journal filed under 31 January 1778 is the issue of 31 March; the printing on it keeps the filed date with a note; a correction release can date it (Q-08).

for_user_decision.Publications counted by their opening (X: As built: Congress's audience of the French minister with the King of France's letter, the address and the President's answer; the King's message with the French ambassador's paper; Congress's proceedings of 6 June with the President's answer: each one item.
for_user_decision.Separate public acts as sub-stories (X-1: As built: Congress's declaration on Mr. Johnstone (4 papers) and the two declarations of 26 August (5 each) as three sub-stories of one parent; the commissioners' requisition of 26 August on the troops of the convention (5 of 6) and Congress's resolution of 4 September answering it (5 of 5) as two sub-stories of another (X-1800-01).
for_user_decision.The King's speech of November 1777 and t: As built: the 'Annotations' quote the speech phrase by phrase and are not counted (C-07); the speech is in 3 papers, below the bar.
for_user_decision.The papers in print and the bar (X-1778-: 8 papers (11 catalogue series); 3 to 7 in print in any three weeks: 4 papers needed in nearly every month, 5 for items printed over weeks in which all 8 survive.
for_user_decision.The sweep for short items (X-1778-08): Run at the year's floor (4 papers); ten eligible items come from it (six in the first count, four more in the recount), none chosen.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1778 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 309 items printed somewhere, 130 in 4 or more catalogue series by the finder's count), and the families of 1777 were looked for on the 1778 pages (items_from_1777.json: 36 items, one in 4 papers). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page (about 100 words of its text, both transcriptions); the items were joined into documents and every document that might reach the bar was counted again by about 70 words from its own opening on a reference page, with every page listed and the doubtful ones read; a sweep of passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 4 or more papers found short items the families miss. 125 candidates were counted this way (outputs/story_discovery_1778/counts_1778.json). The admitted stories were searched with phrase searches over all 970 pages in both transcriptions (phrase_hits.json); every hit not in the ledger was read (recitals of the bills' titles, a second copy of the New-Jersey Gazette of 1 July, other reports naming Count d'Estaing). Each printing was checked against its page scan.

value.paper_counting: 1778 has 11 catalogue series, which are 8 papers (C-04): the Connecticut Courant under three catalogue numbers and the Freeman's Journal / New-Hampshire Gazette under two; the two Williamsburg Virginia Gazettes are two papers. 3 to 7 papers are in print in any three weeks, so an item needs 4 papers in almost every month (5 when its printings span weeks in which all 8 survive).
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (register Y-THIN, chosen by the owner on 23 November 2026 and amended the same night with the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4; the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted (3 in 1778), and the others are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (a target, not a quota); one affair's items are handled as in X-1800-01; the eligible items not chosen are listed here.

counted_item_by_item.A sweep for short items: As in the 1803 review (X-1803-09), every page of 1779 was swept for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 4 or more papers: of 1,538 shared passages, 1,458 lie within the finder's items, 9 are advertisement formulas, and the other 71 were read; the items they hold were counted by their own openings (none of them is chosen).
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains items printed together: Congress's resolutions of 2 January with its address of 13 January and the resolutions of 14 January; the papers from Georgia (General Prevost's proclamation, Colonel White's postscript, Colonel Fuser's summons and the answer); General Moultrie's and General Putnam's letters; General Washington's letters on Stony Point, General Wayne's report, the returns and the thanks of Congress; runs of London, Charlestown and Boston news. Each text was counted by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote, and texts that sh: C-07 and C-06: a page that quotes an item's first sentence inside other text is not counted (the Pennsylvania Packet's meeting resolutions of 3 July quoting Congress's address of 26 May); an extract that leaves out the opening is not counted (the Virginia Gazette's extract of Congress's circular letter of 13 September, which is then in 3 papers and below the bar); different texts that describe the same men in the same words are counted apart (the three texts on Lieutenant Governor Hamilton, each below the bar).
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: By the first 40 words of their openings, the eligible items are as listed in not_admitted (with their counts); one item is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks (the King's speech of 26 November 1778, 7 of 7). The chosen items were counted by phrase searches and every hit read; their counts and the papers that survive for their weeks are in the README's table of stories.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again counts again: C-08: the Pennsylvania Packet printed Congress's resolutions of 2 January in five issues, General Washington's proclamation in four, and the Charlestown report of Colonel Campbell's retreat and Congress's resolutions on prices twice each; the Pennsylvania Packet printed the Spanish manifesto in two forms a week apart.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: C-02: the King of Spain's manifesto in two translations, and once within his own decree from the Madrid Gazette (7 papers); General Putnam's letter printed inside General Washington's letter (3 papers) or alone (1); the account of the attack at Stono Ferry under two headings (an officer's letter, 4; 'authentic intelligence received by his Excellency the Governor', 1).
counted_item_by_item.This year's printings: C-11: the King's speech of 26 November 1778, Colonel Fuser's summons of 25 November 1778 and Congress's resolutions of 19 November 1779 are counted by their printings of 1779.

for_user_decision.A ship lost with her crew: As built (R-04): the Boston report of a brig wrecked in a gale off Plymouth in December 1778, and of her crew's sufferings (4 of the 5 papers that survive for its weeks), turns on private persons and is not admitted without your decision; it is listed under 'for the owner' without names.
for_user_decision.Both sides: As built (R-02): the British commanders' address to the inhabitants of Connecticut, Colonel Fuser's summons, and the reprints of the New-York Gazette, printed in the city the British held, with its own headings and introductions (Governor Livingston, 'titular Governor'; 'Lincoln's Letter to the Congress. Acknowledging the Defeat of the French and Rebels, in Georgia'), are described by whose account they are, in the papers' words.
for_user_decision.General Sullivan's expedition: As built (R-02): the letter from an officer in General Sullivan's army is admitted as that officer's account of the burning of the towns of the Six Nations; its description says that it is not the Six Nations' account.
for_user_decision.Printed forms counted together: As built (C-02): the King of Spain's manifesto in two translations and within his decree (7 papers; the English translation alone, 6); General Putnam's letter with or without General Washington's covering letter (4; with the letter, 3); the Stono Ferry account under two headings (5; as the officer's letter, 4).
for_user_decision.The choice under the amended rule (B1): As built: 27 stories (25 single stories, and 2 parent stories with 5 sub-stories), 161 printings in all 9 papers; one story admitted by the rule's first part (the King's speech), 29 items chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, and the other eligible items listed as not chosen with their counts. Any not-chosen item can be added after a scan check of its printings.
for_user_decision.The single issues of the New-Jersey Jour: As built: each counts among the papers that survive for an item's weeks, as the rule reads. The South Carolina issue of 15 September raises the bar to 5 papers for items whose weeks hold it and the Newport Gazette, and it keeps the King of Spain's manifesto (7 of 8) and the Charlestown paragraph (7 of 8) from being printed by every surviving paper; the New-Jersey Journal's issue of 16 February does the same for Congress's resolutions of 2 January (6 of 7).

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1779 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 625 items printed somewhere; by the finder's count 4 reach 7 papers, 11 reach 6, 60 reach 5 and 156 reach 4). The same script was run with year 1778 over the 1779 pages (items_from_1778.json: 16 items, none in more than 3 papers). Every finder item in 3 or more papers (496) was counted again by its own opening against every page of 1779 in both transcriptions: first by about 100 words, then, because a short item's 100 words take in the paragraph printed after it, by the first 40 words (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams). Items read from different printings of one text were merged, and the parts of one document joined (a letter with the enclosures printed with it, a day's resolutions of Congress under one heading, an address printed in parts). A sweep of the year for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 4 or more papers, as the 1803 review introduced (X-1803-09), found short items the reuse families had not joined; each was counted by its own opening. The 30 chosen items were then counted by their openings with phrase searches over all 1,660 pages of 1779 in both transcriptions, and every hit was read.

value.paper_counting: 1779 has 9 catalogue series, which are 9 papers: no paper is under two catalogue numbers. The Pennsylvania Packet (Philadelphia, three a week), the New-York Gazette, and the Weekly Mercury (New York, held by the British; Mondays), the Connecticut Courant (Hartford; Tuesdays), the New-Jersey Gazette (Trenton; Wednesdays) and the New-Hampshire Gazette (Portsmouth; Tuesdays) run all year; the Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) from 12 February; the Newport Gazette (Newport, held by the British) on 25 March and from 1 July to 6 October; the New-Jersey Journal (Chatham) and the Gazette of the State of South-Carolina (Charlestown) have one issue each (16 February, 15 September). Papers in print in any three weeks: 5 in January, 6 or 7 from February to July, 7 or 8 in August and September, 6 from October; the bar is 4 papers almost all year and 5 where an item's weeks hold both the Newport Gazette and the South Carolina issue. Every count here counts eligible pages of issues the release dates to 1779.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35, a target, not a quota); digests are not admitted. One item of 1779 is printed by every surviving paper: the King's speech of 26 November 1778 (7 of 7). From the other eligible items 29 were chosen, in 26 stories (two parents with five groups), covering every month and the kinds of news of the year (the war in America; Congress, the currency and public life; Britain, Spain and the war at sea). Where several items of one affair reach the bar in the same weeks, the most widely printed is chosen and the others are listed as not chosen, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01): General Washington's two letters on Stony Point and the thanks of Congress are three public acts. Nothing is held back for its subject.

counted_item_by_item.Judgement calls of the reading: Among the items not chosen: Congress's resolutions on Virginia's land office and on peace with the Indian nations reach the bar with two papers printing them in the journal of Congress and two quoting them in news paragraphs; the Viper's return reaches it only with two Boston wordings counted together (C-02); the Dublin paragraph on the Irish Commons stays at 3 papers (a London rewording in the New-York Gazette is not counted); one-sentence London paragraphs are items (C-09); the summons to General Lincoln, printed alone in May, is kept apart from the capitulation papers that reprint it in June; General Gates's publication of September is three items.
counted_item_by_item.Letters printed together: A letter and the papers it sends are one item (X-1810-01): General Washington's letter of 18 January with Lord Stirling's report; General Lincoln's letter of 24 May with the capitulation papers (the Virginia Gazette and the New-Hampshire Gazette print the papers without it, or later); Governor Jefferson's letter of 15 October with the dispatches it encloses (the Virginia Gazette prints the dispatches without it).
counted_item_by_item.Pages that recite or quote an item, or p: Not counted (C-07): Pennsylvania's bill (25 March, 6 June) and New Jersey's act (12 July) that recite Congress's resolutions of 18 March; a letter to the printer of the New-Hampshire Gazette (8 April) quoting the King's speech. Not counted (C-06): the New-Hampshire Gazette's printing of only the later part of the letter from near Morristown of 9 June.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Every finder item of 1780 in 3 or more papers (and of 1779 over the 1780 pages) was counted by its own opening over all 1,406 pages in both transcriptions and merged into text units: 174 units met the bar. Reading them, with the sweep's passages, gave 186 items, 154 eligible; the sweep checked again on 24 November (its coverage test had been too loose) added 38 eligible items, 192 in all. Five are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks and are admitted; 23 are chosen (23 stories, 28 groups, 142 printings); 160 eligible items are listed as not chosen, 4 more that turn on private persons are listed for the owner, and 32 items read are below the bar.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: C-02: General Washington's general orders of 20 July under two introductions (a Chatham extract and an officer's letter of 22 July).
counted_item_by_item.The bar: Y-THIN: more than half of the papers that survive for the item's weeks (a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and at least 4. 1780 has 7 papers; 6 are in print in most weeks and 7 in the weeks of 20 June, when the Royal South-Carolina Gazette's one surviving issue counts; the bar is 4.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1780 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 513 items printed somewhere), and the families of 1779 were looked for on the 1780 pages (items_from_1779.json: 72 items). Every item in 3 or more papers was counted by its own opening over all 1,406 pages in both transcriptions and merged into text units (174 met the bar); every page was swept for seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers (87 passages no item covers, read; 13 items added); every unit that meets the bar was read, and the chosen items' openings were searched over all pages.

value.paper_counting: 1780 has 7 catalogue series, which are 7 papers: the Pennsylvania Packet, the New-Jersey Gazette, the New-York Gazette (New York, under the British), the Connecticut Courant, the Virginia Gazette, the New-Hampshire Gazette and the Royal South-Carolina Gazette (one issue, Charleston, 20 June). The release's map lists no misfiled RevX page for 1780; no 1780 issue has a corrected date.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (register Y-THIN) as amended by the owner's choice B1 on 23 November 2026: an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4; digests are not. As in R-01, items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35, a target, not a quota); one affair's items as in X-1800-01. The eligible items not chosen are listed with their counts and are not checked against the scans. Sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) apply as in every year.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted by their own words and joined into documents, 181 items of 1781 are eligible: 123 in 4 papers, 43 in 5, 15 in 6. 14 items are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks and are admitted; 13 more are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; together, with their introductions and later passages, they are 36 of the eligible documents. 145 eligible items are not chosen and are listed with their counts and their own opening words. 226 more documents of the item finder are in 3 papers or fewer by their own words, below the bar (docs_1781.json); they are not listed one by one.
counted_item_by_item.Titles of the items not chosen: Each eligible item not chosen is listed by its own words: the dateline or heading before the finder's position and the words that follow (some begin inside the item, where the finder's position does); a notice that names a private person is described instead.

for_user_decision.A printing counts where its opening surv: As built (C-06): the proposals made to the soldiers of the Pennsylvania line are in 3 papers by their opening; the New-York Gazette's page of 12 February begins in the middle of them, so the item is below the bar.
for_user_decision.Choosing among the eligible items (X-178: As built (B1): 14 items printed by every surviving paper admitted, 13 chosen by month and kind with one affair's items as X-1800-01 (25 stories in all), 145 not chosen and listed with their counts.
for_user_decision.Filing and dates (X-1781-08): Data: the Royal Gazette of Charleston heads each issue 'From Saturday ... to Wednesday ...' (or the reverse) and is filed under the first day, 3 or 4 days before it was issued; filed dates kept. The Pennsylvania Packet of 11 October (No. 793) is filed correctly; its list of letters dated 'October 5, 1782' is the printer's misprint.
for_user_decision.Notices and titles of the items not chos: As built: eligible items that are notices or advertisements are not chosen (C-10); every eligible item not chosen is listed by its own opening words.
for_user_decision.Pages that quote an item, or print it in: As built (C-07): a letter in the Connecticut Courant of 3 April that recites the order for reprisals, and a notice in the Pennsylvania Packet of 4 and 11 August that quotes Congress's resolution of 23 July, are not printings; nor is the Royal Gazette's account of the action of 16 March in other words (27 June); the New-Jersey Gazette of 9 May prints another order in council, of 22 December 1780, not the order of 20 December again.
for_user_decision.Papers printed under the British (X-1781: As built: the New-York Gazette and the Royal Gazette of Charleston counted like the other papers; their headings and comments described as theirs.
for_user_decision.Printed again counts again (X-1781-03): As built (C-08): the Pennsylvania Packet's two of General Washington's letter of 19 October, and of the London paragraph on the Eustatius convoy.
for_user_decision.Publications counted by their opening (X: As built: General Washington's letter of 19 October with the correspondence and the articles of capitulation; the Marquis de Lafayette's letter to General Greene printed after his covering letter to Congress; General Morgan's letter as General Greene sent it to Congress; the plan for a national bank with the papers printed with it: each one item, counted by its opening (X-1810-01).
for_user_decision.Separate public acts as sub-stories (X-1: As built: the King's manifesto against the United Provinces (5 papers) and the order of 20 December 1780 for general reprisals (6 of 6) under one parent; General Washington's letter of 19 October (6 of 6) and Lord Cornwallis's letter to Sir Henry Clinton (5) under another (X-1800-01).
for_user_decision.The papers in print and the bar (X-1781-: 7 catalogue series, 6 papers; the Royal Gazette of Charleston from March; 5 or 6 papers in print in any three weeks, so an item needs 4 papers all year.
for_user_decision.Two resolutions of Congress of 29 Octobe: As built: the thanks of Congress to General Washington and the French commanders are in 3 papers by their own words, and its thanks of the same day to Major General Greene in 2; both are below the bar and listed. Counted by their shared opening formula they had been joined (4 papers); the scan check showed the difference.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1781 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 653 items printed somewhere, 245 in 4 or more catalogue series by the finder's count), and the families of 1780 were looked for on the 1781 pages (items_from_1780.json: 45 items, 5 in 4 or more). Every item in 3 or more papers was counted by machine by about 100 words of its text from the finder's position, over all 1,623 pages in both transcriptions (a dense run of its word 5-grams, at least a quarter of them); the counts were joined into documents (items standing together on most of the same pages). The admitted and chosen items were counted again by about 70 words from their own opening (counts_1781.json), and the pages that only quote or recite them were read and left out. Each admitted printing was checked against its page scan.

value.paper_counting: 1781 has 7 catalogue series, which are 6 papers (C-04): the Portsmouth New-Hampshire Gazette under two catalogue numbers (sn83025584 to 3 September, sn83025585 from 8 September). The Royal Gazette of Charleston survives from March; 5 or 6 papers are in print in any three weeks, so an item needs 4 papers all year.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (register Y-THIN, chosen by the owner on 23 November 2026 and amended the same night with the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4; the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted (14 in 1781), and the others are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (a target, not a quota); one affair's items are handled as in X-1800-01; the eligible items not chosen are listed here.

counted_item_by_item.A letter and what it encloses: General Washington's letter of 10 May is counted with Sir Guy Carleton's letter that it encloses; General Greene's letters of 28 and 29 August with General Leslie's letter and General Gist's report; General Greene's letter of 31 May with General Wayne's letter, which the New-Hampshire Gazette prints alone (as X-1810-01, and 1779's General Putnam letter, X-1779-03).
counted_item_by_item.Extracts without the opening: Not counted (C-06): the New-Hampshire Gazette's extract of the letter from Paris of 9 August (its second paragraph, under the same heading), and its extract of General Greene's letter of 31 May ('Flying parties of the British cavalry ...'), printed after it had printed General Wayne's letter.
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains items printed together: the King's speech of 27 November 1781 with the addresses of both Houses, the King's answer to the Lords and Lord Cornwallis's letter; General Greene's letters of 21 and 31 May; Congress's resolutions of 4 October with General Greene's letters of August. Each was counted apart by its own opening.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote or recite an item: Not counted (C-07): papers that quote Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby's letter inside other texts in October to December; states' proclamations that recite Congress's proclamation of thanksgiving; a state assembly's resolutions in the Connecticut Courant of 29 October that repeat the preamble of Congress's resolutions of 4 October; the New-Jersey Journal's comment that quotes the King's speech of 27 November 1781.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: By the first 40 words of their openings, the eligible items not chosen are as listed in not_admitted (with their counts). The admitted and chosen items were counted by phrase searches of their openings and every hit read; their counts and the papers that survive for their weeks are in the README's table of stories.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again counts again: The Pennsylvania Packet printed the orders of 10 January in six issues, and the King's speech of 27 November 1781, Lord Cornwallis's letter, Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby's letter and Congress's resolutions of 4 October twice each.

for_user_decision.A letter with its enclosure, printed in: As built: General Greene's letter of 31 May with General Wayne's letter is printed by all five papers that survive for its weeks, counting the New-Hampshire Gazette, which prints General Wayne's letter alone; without that printing it is in 4 of 5 and would be chosen, not admitted by the first part.
for_user_decision.Both sides: As built (R-02): the Royal Gazette of Charleston's own report of Savannah's evacuation, the British commanders' letters (Lord Cornwallis, Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby, General Leslie) and Governor Elliot's letter as a Cork paper printed it are admitted and described as theirs; the Amsterdam handbill as the papers describe it.
for_user_decision.Digests among the items printed by every: As built (C-09): the news by the ship Apollo (4 of 4), the substance of the Leyden papers (printed in parts), the news a Salem cartel brought, and the news by the ship Carolina (4 of 4, one paper rewording its first sentence) are runs of unrelated reports and are not admitted, as 1805's news by the Palmyra and 1808's by the Camilla.
for_user_decision.Extracts without the opening: As built (C-06): the letter from Paris of 9 August and the Paris paragraph on Mr. Franklin and Mr. Jay with the Count de Aranda are each in 3 of the 4 surviving papers by their openings, below the bar.
for_user_decision.Single surviving issues: As built (as X-1779-02): the New-York Gazette's 2 issues, the Royal South-Carolina Gazette's 3 and the New-Jersey Journal's 9 count among the papers that survive for an item's weeks when they fall in its window.
for_user_decision.The choice under the amended rule (B1): As built: 13 items chosen in 11 stories (General Greene's letter of 21 May is a sub-story of an admitted parent; Congress's resolutions of 12 August stand with Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby's letter under a parent), so that every month from January to September has a story; the other eligible items listed as not chosen with their counts. Any not-chosen item can be added after a scan check of its printings.
for_user_decision.The first part in the autumn: As built: 22 items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, 19 of them from September to December, when only the four year-round papers (the Pennsylvania Packet, the Connecticut Courant, the New-Jersey Gazette and the New-Hampshire Gazette) survive; with the 11 chosen stories, 30 stories in all. The rule's first part reads 'every newspaper that survives for their weeks', however few survive; the audit could ask for more papers (Y-THIN, 'Reopen if').

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1782 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 550 items printed somewhere). The same script was run with year 1781 over the 1782 pages (items_from_1781.json: 47 items, 5 of them in 4 or more papers by the finder's count). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1782 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (395 texts). For every text at the bar or one paper short of it, the papers the comparison missed were looked for again on their pages (the best page within the text's weeks) and read. A sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers, over every page, found items the families miss (as X-1803-09); each was read. Every admitted and chosen item was then counted by phrase searches of its opening over all 1,509 pages in both transcriptions, and every hit read (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).

value.paper_counting: 1782 has 8 catalogue series, which are 8 papers: no paper is under two catalogue numbers. The Pennsylvania Packet (Philadelphia, three a week, 157 issues), the Connecticut Courant (Hartford; Tuesdays, 53), the New-Jersey Gazette (Trenton; Wednesdays, 52) and the New-Hampshire Gazette and General Advertiser (Portsmouth; Saturdays, 52) run all year; the Royal Gazette (Charleston, held by the British) to 3 August (62 issues); the New-Jersey Journal (Chatham) survives in 9 issues, the Royal South-Carolina Gazette (Charleston) in 3 and the New-York Gazette, and the Weekly Mercury (New York, held by the British) in 2. Papers in print in any three weeks: 4 to 7; 7 in March, 5 or 6 in most windows from January to July, and only the four year-round papers in 67 windows, most of them from August on.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35, a target, not a quota); digests are not admitted. In 1782, 22 items are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks, 19 of them from September to December, when only the four year-round papers survive; 13 items are chosen, in 11 stories, so that every month from January to September has one.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Of 47 items eligible by the count, 18 reach every paper that survives for their weeks; read again by their own words, all 18 do (17 in 4 of 4, one in 5 of 5) and are admitted. 8 are chosen; the others are listed as not chosen, except one item on a private person, listed for the owner, and the definitive treaty, below the bar by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: The New-Hampshire Gazette's state of the Jamaica convoy, the New-Jersey Gazette's report of the French frigate, the New-Hampshire Gazette's Lisbon paragraph in other words, and Congress's proclamation as the New-Jersey Gazette prints it within a New Jersey proclamation (C-02).

value.paper_counting: 1783 has 9 catalogue series, which are 9 papers: the Pennsylvania Packet (122 issues, to 11 October), the New-Hampshire Gazette (51), the Connecticut Courant (41, to 9 December) and the New-Jersey Gazette (29) carry most of the year; the Gazette of the State of South-Carolina survives from 16 July, the New-Jersey Journal in 4 issues to 9 April, and three Charleston papers in 6 issues of April and May. No 1783 issue has a corrected date; the release's map lists no misfiled RevX page of 1783.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN, as amended on 23 November 2026, the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; as in R-01, the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35); one affair's items as in X-1800-01; digests are not admitted; sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) as in every year. In 1783 4 to 7 papers survive for the weeks of every item in the ledger, so the bar is 4 for each; from mid-October fewer than 4 papers survive and no item can be eligible.

counted_item_by_item.Letters printed together: A letter and the papers it sends are one item (X-1810-01): the Constitution, the Convention's resolutions and General Washington's letter (the Independent Journal's supplement prints the letter first); Mr. Jay's letter and the note that sends it to the printer (the New-Hampshire Gazette prints the letter without the note).
counted_item_by_item.Pages that quote an item or print a late: Not counted (C-07): the Daily Advertiser's printing of Congress's resolution of 21 February inside an essay by Cato (15 October); the New-York Journal's essays that quote the Constitution at length (18 October and later); the reports of the Pennsylvania convention that quote Mr. Mason's objections. Not counted (C-06): the Kentucke Gazette's printing of only the later articles of the treaty with Morocco (18 August, 'continued from our last'); the New-Hampshire Gazette's printing of only the later part of the requisition, with the quotas (21 November).
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Every finder item of 1787 in 3 or more papers (and of 1786 over the 1787 pages: none) was counted by its own opening over all 1,297 pages in both transcriptions and merged into text units: 33 of 123 units met the bar, of which 7 are advertisements and legal notices and 13 are parts of the Constitution. Reading them, with the sweep's passages, gave 25 items read: 15 eligible and 10 below the bar (with The Federalist's numbers, each in 3 papers, as one line). Three are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks and are admitted; 10 are chosen (13 stories, 13 groups, 54 printings); 1 eligible item is listed as not chosen and 1 for the owner.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again: C-08: the New-Hampshire Gazette reports the judges of the western territory again on 9 November, in its own words under Portsmouth.

counted_item_by_item.The acts of Congress by their own words: The automatic families join the acts of the session by their formulas ('Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives'); counted by each act's opening, the acts on Kentucky, on Vermont and on another regiment are in 4 papers each, and the excise act, the Bank's supplementary act and the act fixing the next meeting of Congress in 3 (below the bar); pages that only recite an act's title, such as the New-Hampshire Gazette's list of the session's acts of 16 June, are not counted (C-07).
counted_item_by_item.The window of the Danville letter: The Danville letter is printed from 17 September to 7 October; the Kentucky Gazette's next issue after 23 July is of 8 October, the day after the letter's three weeks (Y-THIN counts the first printing's day and the 20 days after it). So 4 papers survive for its weeks, and the letter, printed by all 4, is admitted.

for_user_decision.Printed forms counted together: As built (X-1791-03): General Scott's account, the letter from Paris, the King of France's letter and the Hardy paragraph, each with its other forms (C-02); counted apart, none of the first three would reach the bar.
for_user_decision.Separate public papers of one affair: As built (X-1791-04): the President's speech and both Houses' answers; the acts on Kentucky and on Vermont; General Scott's circular and General St. Clair's report on the defeat of the army (X-1800-01).
for_user_decision.The acts of Congress by their own words: As built (X-1791-02): each act counted by its own opening; the excise act is below the bar (3 papers).
for_user_decision.The choice for 1791: As built (X-1791-01): 6 groups admitted by the rule's first part and 16 chosen, 18 stories and 98 printings; the other eligible items are listed as not chosen.
for_user_decision.The window's edge: As built (X-1791-05): the Danville letter's weeks end the day before the Kentucky Gazette's next issue; 4 papers survive and the letter is admitted.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1791 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json), and again with the families of 1790 over the 1791 pages (items_from_1790.json). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page and counted again by its opening; a sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers found the runs no finder item covers, and they were read. Counted item by item (80 entries, the daily proceedings of Congress left out as digests), 67 items meet the bar (count_1791.md); where an item's family or run also holds other texts (the acts of Congress share their formulas), its papers were counted by its own words. The admitted and chosen items were counted again by their own words over all 1,242 pages in both transcriptions, and read on every page.
