value.paper_counting: 1791 has 6 catalogue series, which are 6 papers: the Gazette of the United States (107 issues), the New-Hampshire Gazette (53), the New Hampshire Gazetteer (49) and the Patowmac Guardian (49) through the year; the Kentucky Gazette (41), with no issue from 23 July to 8 October; and the National Gazette (18) from 31 October. No 1791 issue has a corrected date; the release's map lists 3 misfiled RevX pages of 1791 (the New-Hampshire Gazette of 12 February and 1 September), none of them a page of this ledger.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN, as amended on 23 November 2026, the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; as in R-01, the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35); one affair's items as in X-1800-01; digests are not admitted; sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) as in every year. In 1791 4 to 6 papers survive for an item's weeks, so the bar is 4 for every item.

counted_item_by_item.Acts of Congress: The acts on the post-office, the protection of the frontiers, the mint and the militia are counted by their printings whole from the title; the lists of the session's acts that name them, and the House proceedings on their bills, are not counted (C-07).
counted_item_by_item.Counted by their own words and opening: C-06 and C-07, from reading every printing of the chosen items and of the items they were weighed against: the French King's speech of 20 April is printed from its opening by 3 papers (the Potowmac Guardian prints only its conclusion, X-1802-06) and the Brussels accounts of 4 and 10 May by 3 each (other papers give the same news in their own words or in other paragraphs): below the bar. The Paris paragraph on Paul Jones (the National Gazette's is its own summary) and the letter from Ostend on M. La Fayette (the National Gazette prints only the paragraph that follows it) are printed by 4 of the 5 papers in print, not all; Mr. Seagrove's letter by 4 papers (a Philadelphia paragraph that sums it up, in 3, is not counted).
counted_item_by_item.Letters printed together: X-1810-01: the President's letter of 16 January and the Secretary of War's statement; the President's message of 5 March and the King of France's letter.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Every finder item of 1792 in 3 or more papers (and of 1791 over the 1792 pages) was counted by its own opening over all 1,629 pages in both transcriptions and merged into text units: 176 of 428 units met the bar. Reading them, with the sweep's passages, gave 236 items, and 2 more were read beside the chosen ones (238): 188 eligible and 50 below the bar. Four are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks and are admitted; 25 are chosen (29 stories, 29 groups, 146 printings); 142 eligible items are listed as not chosen and 17 for the owner.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again: C-08: the Potowmac Guardian prints the President's proclamation of September twice and the Kentucky Gazette five times; each printing counts (the 146 printings include them).
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms together: C-02: the Charleston paragraph on Mr. Bowles ('By a letter received in town from the Rock Landing', and 'A Charleston paper mentions, that'); the Baltimore report from Cape-Francois (the Potowmac Guardian's 'The last accounts from Cape Francois state', under Boston); the report of the Five Nations' deputation (as the Albany Gazette's, as a gentleman's from the Genesee country, and as an addition to another paragraph); the Paris paragraph on Paul Jones (two papers print it among deaths); the Dublin letter (two papers print it under Dublin without 'Extract of a letter'); the Petersburg paragraph (the Kentucky Gazette dates it Richmond, 5 May); the decree against M. La Fayette (the National Gazette gives the account before it in its own words).
counted_item_by_item.The Kentucky Gazette as edition 2: The archive files the Kentucky Gazette's 1792 issues as edition 2 (the issue of 7 January also as edition 1); the ledger uses the release's keys.
counted_item_by_item.The bar: Y-THIN: more than half of the papers that survive for the item's weeks (a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and at least 4. 1792 has 8 papers: the National Gazette, the Gazette of the United States, the New-Hampshire Gazette, the New Hampshire Gazetteer, the Kentucky Gazette and the Potowmac Guardian survive for the whole year (the Kentucky Gazette has no issue in October), the Mirrour from 6 September (none in October), and the Phenix in one issue, 26 December. The bar is 4, and 5 when the Phenix's issue falls in an item's weeks.

for_user_decision.Choosing among the eligible items (X-179: As built: each month's most widely printed item is chosen; within a month and a kind of news no chosen item is printed by fewer papers than one not chosen, except public acts (the acts of Congress on the post-office, the mint and the militia, the National Assembly's decree of war, Mr. Seagrove's letter as agent); one affair's items in the same weeks as X-1800-01 (M. La Fayette's fall: the Assembly's decree of accusation, not the letter from Ostend or the paragraph declaring him a traitor; the Knoxville paper of 10 October: its statement on the Spanish governors, not its account of the attack on Buchanan's station; Mr. Bowles in March and April). An anecdote (General Stark's, February, 5 papers) is not chosen (C-10). 29 stories, about a standard year's number.
for_user_decision.Counts corrected by reading every printi: As built (C-06, C-07): six items' counts are lower than the reading's: the French King's speech of 20 April and the Brussels accounts of 4 and 10 May fall below the bar; the paragraph on Paul Jones and the letter from Ostend are printed by 4 of the 5 papers in print, not all; Mr. Seagrove's letter by 4 papers, not 6. The other eligible items not chosen keep the reading's counts and are not checked against the scans.
for_user_decision.Data issues (X-1792-04): As built: the Gazette of the United States of Wednesday 5 December (No. 54) is filed under 3 December; the release's map already gives other pages' RevX text for the Gazette of 1 December and the National Gazette of 26 December (pages 1 to 3); the Kentucky Gazette of 9 June has 6 pages (pages 5 and 6 are advertisements without a masthead); the New Hampshire Gazetteer prints 'Numb. 14' on 5 and 12 October (its later numbers follow the second); RevX reads the Mirrour of 26 November as 'Monday, November 25'. No chosen printing is on these issues. A filing correction can date the Gazette of 5 December as printed at the owner's word.
for_user_decision.Private persons (X-1792-03): As built (R-04): 17 eligible items turn on private persons and are listed for the owner without names; none is needed to cover its month. Three of them (June and July) are about the King of Sweden's assassin, his sentence and his execution: the killing of a king is a public affair, and at the owner's word they can be listed as eligible and not chosen instead.
for_user_decision.The papers in print, the bar and the cho: As built: Y-THIN as amended (B1) with 8 papers (8 catalogue series); the bar of 4 (5 in the last week of December) makes 188 items eligible. Four are printed by every paper in print and admitted; 25 others are chosen (29 stories, 29 groups, 146 printings); 142 are listed as not chosen and 17 for the owner.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1792 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json), and the families of 1791 were split again over the 1792 pages (items_from_1791.json). Every item in 3 or more papers was counted by its own opening over all 1,629 pages in both transcriptions and merged into text units (176 of 428 met the bar); every page was swept for seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers (sweep_new and sweep_recheck: the passages no item covers); every unit and passage that meets the bar was read, and the chosen items' openings were searched over all pages (phrase_hits.json).

value.paper_counting: 1792 has 8 catalogue series, which are 8 papers: the National Gazette and the Gazette of the United States (Philadelphia), the New-Hampshire Gazette, and the General Advertiser (Portsmouth), the New Hampshire Gazetteer (Exeter), the Kentucky Gazette (Lexington), the Potowmac Guardian, and Berkeley Advertiser (its own news is dated at Martinsburg; the catalogue places it at Shepherdstown), the Mirrour (Concord, from 6 September) and the Phenix (Dover, one issue, 26 December). The release's map lists six misfiled RevX pages for 1792 (X-1792-04).
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (register Y-THIN) as amended by the owner's choice B1 on 23 November 2026: an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4; digests are not. As in R-01, items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35, a target, not a quota); one affair's items as in X-1800-01. The eligible items not chosen are listed with their counts and are not checked against the scans. Sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) apply as in every year.

counted_item_by_item.Dampierre's death: The commissioners' letter of 9 May follows their letter of 8 May on the attack (4 papers), which is not part of the group. The Kentucky Gazette's two scanned copies of 14 September count once.
counted_item_by_item.Hamilton's circular and the President's: The circular of 4 August and the schedule of rules sent with it are one publication, counted once: 6 papers (NGz, GUS, NHG, AHL, MIR, EAG). Not in PG, CI or KG.
counted_item_by_item.The Tournai bulletin: NGz and GUS print it as the London Gazette's 'TOURNAI (Tournay), May 3'; NHG, AHL, MIR and PG print the same sentences after a paragraph on the preparations against Condé. PG printed it twice (22 July and 5 August).
counted_item_by_item.The list of the powers at war with Franc: Printed with two introductions to one list: 'An account of the Kings, Princes, and States engaged against the Republic of France' (GUS, NGz, PG) and 'a list of the combination of Kings, Princes, and States, at war with France' (NHG, AHL, MIR). The list is one item, so they are counted together: 6 papers (3 + 3), a judgement call.

value.method: Round two of 1793. Round one (release v0.10.0) admitted the stories with an item in 7 or more papers and proposed a 6-paper threshold for this year, because 1793 has only 6 to 8 papers in print at a time; the owner agreed on 2026-11-10. The candidates in 6 papers that round one listed were read again with phrase searches over all 1,751 pages of 1793 in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns_round2.json, phrase_hits_round2.json), every hit was read, papers in print without a hit were searched with loose keywords, and every admitted printing was checked against its page scan (SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points_round2.json).

not_admitted.Left out for framing (6 papers): The War Office paragraph on the treaty commissioners at the Rapids of the Miami, the German Creek letter on a raid on the 'valley Indian towns', Captain Fanning's account of the burning of Cap Francais and the brig Mary's report of the dead there; they need framing first (outputs/story_discovery_1793/README.md).
not_admitted.Not recommended at 6 papers: The Rome paragraph of 29 September 1792 and the Paris 'sullen tranquillity' paragraph (single digest paragraphs, in months already covered) and Captain Hacket's Amsterdam rumour (two wordings, 4 + 2).

value.selection_rule: For 1793 only, a story needs one printed item found in 6 or more newspapers, counted item by item, with the two titles of a renamed paper counted once and both scanned copies of a Kentucky Gazette issue counted once. Items that need framing stay out, and items in 6 papers were chosen, as items in 7 or 8 papers are in other years, to cover the months and kinds of news: single paragraphs of news digests that add neither (the Rome paragraph of 29 September 1792, the Paris 'sullen tranquillity' paragraph) and a rumour in two wordings (Captain Hacket's report that Dumouriez had taken Amsterdam, 4 + 2 papers) were not admitted. Dumouriez's address, in 6 papers, was already a sub-story of round one.

counted_item_by_item.Cap Français: Captain Fanning's account (New York, 9 July; NGz 10 July, NHG and AHL 16 July, MIR and PG 22 July, GUS on the issue filed under 23 July, which is of 13 July: 6 papers) and the brig Mary's passengers' report (GUS 27 July, NGz 31 July, PG 5 August, NHG and AHL 6 August, CI 14 August: 6 papers) are two items about the same days; each reaches the threshold and each is its own group under the parent 'News from Cap Français, June 1793'.
counted_item_by_item.The German Creek letter: 6 papers (NGz and GUS 11 September, PG 16 September, NHG and AHL 24 September, CI 2 October); PG prints it from a Georgetown paper of 7 September.
counted_item_by_item.The War Office paragraph: 6 papers (NGz 4 September, GUS 7 September, PG 16 September, NHG and AHL 17 September, CI 25 September). Two other items on the commissioners are in 3 papers each and not part of the group: their letter from the mouth of Detroit river (GUS, PG, AHL twice) and a paragraph on the nations' answer of 2 August (NGz, PG, CI).

value.method: Round three of 1793. On 11 November 2026 the owner set the rule 'every story alike': a reviewed story is described by what kind of text it is and whose account, in the papers' own words, never as what happened; sensitive subjects get no special treatment. Items that earlier rounds held back for framing are therefore counted by the year's own rule, exactly like any other item: what reaches it is admitted, what does not stays out. As before, an excerpt ends before the names of private people where it can, and stories that turn on private people stay out. The items rounds one and two left out for framing were read again with phrase searches over all 1,751 pages of 1793 in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns_round3.json, phrase_hits_round3.json), every hit was read, the papers in print without a hit were searched with loose keywords (no missed printing), and every admitted printing was checked against its page scan by AI reviewers (scan_batches/batch_09.json and batch_10.json, SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points_round3.json).

not_admitted.Private people (5 papers each): The prosecutions of the seamen Singleterry and Henfield, and a killing near Middletown, New Jersey: below the threshold, and stories that turn on private people stay out.
not_admitted.The Fugitive Slave Act: 'An act respecting fugitives from justice, and persons escaping from the service of their masters': its text is in 2 papers (MIR 11 March, GUS 17 April); its title is also in the lists of the session's acts (NGz 6 March, GUS 9 March, KG 13 April), which are a different item. Below the threshold.
not_admitted.The civil commissioners' proclamation of: 4 papers (NGz and GUS 27 July, NHG and AHL 13 August; NGz quotes it again in a commentary of 21 August): below the threshold, and not a sub-story, as for the 4-paper documents of Dumouriez's defection.
not_admitted.The letter of Polverel and Sonthonax to: 4 papers (GUS 29 May, NGz 1 June, AHL 18 June, MIR 24 June): below the threshold.

value.selection_rule: For 1793 a story needs one printed item found in 6 or more newspapers, counted item by item, the two titles of a renamed paper once (the owner's decision of 10 November 2026). Where several items belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story; a sub-story may have fewer papers than the threshold when its parent reaches it. As for the 4-paper documents of Dumouriez's defection in round one, items in 4 papers are not admitted as sub-stories.

counted_item_by_item.Genet's letter and the answer: Genet's letter of 13 August and the Secretary of State's answer of 16 August were printed together in all seven papers. They are two signed documents, each its own group under a parent, with Jay and King's statement, which the letter answers, as a third group.
counted_item_by_item.Giles's resolutions on the Secretary of: The item finder counts 7 papers and 17 printings. The resolutions as moved are in GUS 2 Mar, NGz 6 Mar, MIR 18 Mar and NHGA 19 Mar, and as the House journal of 28 February and 1 March in NGz 3 and 6 Apr, NHG 23 Apr and AHL 14 May: 6 catalogue numbers but 5 papers, because NHGA and NHG are one paper. The Kentucky Gazette prints only the debate, in which speakers quote single resolutions; votes and speeches in GUS and NGz were not counted.
counted_item_by_item.Neighbouring paragraphs and chained item: The finder joins neighbouring paragraphs of a news column into chains: the Brussels paragraph of 17 October 1792 stands beside a Rome paragraph (6 papers) and a paragraph on the suttlers of Clairfayt's army (5); the Madeira paragraph is chained to the Philadelphia paragraphs after it in GUS. Each group here is the single item. Dumouriez's address was split by the finder into five items and Saxe-Cobourg's two proclamations into four; they are one document and two documents.
counted_item_by_item.Quotations: Pages that only quote or answer an item were not counted: Jay and King's statement quoted in NGz 24 Aug, 4 and 21 Sep and in their own later statement (PG 23 Dec), and commented on in PG 2 Sep and CI 28 Aug.
counted_item_by_item.Two settings of one paragraph: The Sun paragraph of 10 April is printed with a New York introduction ('In the Sun, of the 10th April, which is the latest paper received') in GUS, NGz (1 June), PG and NHG, and among London paragraphs in NGz (29 May), AHL, MIR and KG; the paragraph itself is the same and is counted as one item.

data_issues.A second scan filed under another date: Pages 3 and 4 filed under the American Herald of Liberty of 2 July 1793 are a second scan of the 9 July issue's pages 3 and 4 (page 3 prints 'BOSTON, JULY 3' and the 9 July heading). No admitted printing is on them (page_date_flags.csv).
data_issues.Misdated issues: Two Gazette of the United States issues are filed under dates their mastheads contradict, confirmed on the scans: the issue filed under 4 April 1793 is Saturday 4 May (Whole No. 419), and the one filed under 23 July is Saturday 13 July (No. 439). No admitted printing is on them (masthead_dates.csv).
data_issues.Misfiled RevX pages: Two 1793 issues have RevX transcriptions filed one page off (Kentucky Gazette 6 April, edition 2; the Mirrour, 22 April). No admitted printing is on them.
data_issues.The Kentucky Gazette of 1793: Its 1793 mastheads agree with the filed dates (all 67 front pages read, both copies counted: 64 agree, and the other 3 are misread or misprinted days), unlike the Kentucky Gazette and General Advertiser of 1806 to 1808. Most issues were scanned twice (editions 1 and 2).

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1793 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running, families of 3 or more papers rather than the default 4, because 1793 has few papers in print), were split into single printed items (items.json: 10 items in 7 papers, none in 8 or more, 22 in exactly 6). The script was also run with year 1792 over the 1793 pages (items_from_1792.json); none of those items reaches 6 papers. Two AI reviewers (Claude Fable) read the items of each half of the year in 4 or more papers and proposed the stories; each item's printings were looked for with phrase searches over all 1,751 pages of 1793 in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json), and every hit was read. Papers with pages in a story's weeks but no printing were searched with loose keywords. Every admitted printing was then checked against its page scan (SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points.json).

not_admitted.Below 6 papers: The Ostend news by the ship Fortitude (5), Jefferson's letter to the Philadelphia merchants on spoliations (5), Marat's funeral (5), the Convention's decree arresting foreigners (5, a digest paragraph), the revocation of vice-consul Duplaine's exequatur and Genet's answer (4 each), Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation of 9 April (5), Dumouriez's letter from Louvain (4), the ship William (5), and others listed in the README.
not_admitted.Candidates in 6 papers: Proposed to the owner under a 6-paper threshold, not admitted: the list of the powers at war with France (two introductions, 3 + 3), the London Gazette bulletin from Tournai of 3 May, Hamilton's circular to the collectors with the President's rules on neutrality, the declaration of the President of the National Convention on a plot, the Cadiz letter of 24 June, the commissioners' letter on General Dampierre's death, and (needing framing) the War Office paragraph on the treaty commissioners at the Rapids of the Miami. Weaker: the Rome paragraph and the Paris 'sullen tranquillity' paragraph (digest paragraphs) and Captain Hacket's Amsterdam rumour (two wordings, 4 + 2).
not_admitted.Left out for framing: The German Creek letter on a raid on the 'valley Indian towns' (6 papers), Captain Fanning's account of the burning of Cap Francais (6), the brig Mary's report of the dead at Cap Francais (6), the civil commissioners' proclamation giving liberty to the 'negro warriors' (4), the Fugitive Slave Act (its text in 2 papers), the letter of Polverel and Sonthonax to Genet (4), the prosecutions of Singleterry and Henfield (5; private seamen) and a killing near Middletown, New Jersey (5; private people).
not_admitted.The 1793 news that no single item carrie: The execution of Louis XVI (six different accounts, none in more than 5 of the 6 papers then in print), France's decree of war on Britain and Holland (5), the French Republic's letter to the United States (5), Giles's resolutions (5 papers), the neutrality proclamation (4 papers by its own text), Washington's second inauguration (4), Genet's arrival and the addresses to him (2 to 4 each), the yellow fever in Philadelphia (no shared item above 4 papers), Toulon (no item above 4), the President's address of 3 December (4 papers, all those then in print) and the Algerine captures (Church's circular, 3).

value.selection_rule: As for 1776, 1807 and 1808: a story needs one printed item found in 7 or more newspapers, counted item by item. No item of 1793 reaches 8 papers; every non-digest item in 7 papers was admitted. Where several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story, and a sub-story may have fewer than 7 papers when its parent reaches 7 (the rule the owner agreed for 1776 round two): Dumouriez's address (6 papers), Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation of 5 April (5) and Jay and King's statement on Genet (5). The two titles of one renamed paper (the New-Hampshire Gazette at Portsmouth; Ranlet's paper at Exeter, the New Hampshire Gazetteer and then the American Herald of Liberty) were never counted twice toward a threshold; no admitted story's count depends on them. Both scanned copies of a Kentucky Gazette issue count once. A paper that printed an item again counts each printing. A 6-paper threshold for this year is proposed in the README and was not applied.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted by their own words, 366 items of 1794 are eligible: 247 in 4 papers, 102 in 5, 16 in 6, 1 in 7. 27 items are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks and are admitted; 8 more are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news (one affair's three items under a parent story). 10 more eligible items counted by their opening are not chosen, and 321 documents of the item finder are eligible by their own words and not chosen; all are listed with their counts. 6 candidates counted by their opening are below the bar and listed. 427 more documents of the item finder are in 3 papers or fewer by their own words, below the bar (docs_1794.json); they are not listed one by one.
counted_item_by_item.Titles of the items not chosen: Each eligible document of the item finder not chosen is listed by its own words: the dateline or heading before the finder's position and the words that follow (some begin inside the item, where the finder's position does); a notice or advertisement that names a private person is described instead (R-04). Each candidate counted by its opening is listed by a title of the review's.

for_user_decision.A printing counts where its opening surv: As built (C-06): the American Herald prints the opening of the Brussels paragraph of 16 March at the foot of a page and the rest on the next, and its printing stands on the first page; the Patowmac Guardian's page of 28 July is torn at the top, and the Paris paragraph of 27 May has lost its dateline and first words there, so that printing does not count and the paragraph is in 5 of the 6 papers that survive for its weeks.
for_user_decision.A shipmaster named in a report (X-1794-0: As built: the Boston report that Captain Talbot, an American whose brig was taken, cruises against British vessels under a French commission is admitted (5 of 5) and names him as the papers print him, as a shipmaster acting in public affairs (as Captain Fanning in 1793). Say if you want it held for your decision instead (R-04).
for_user_decision.Another text that shares the words (X-17: As built (C-07): Britain's instructions of 8 January 1794 recite those of November 1793 and are counted on their own (3 papers, below the bar); the instructions of November are in 5 papers by their opening.
for_user_decision.Choosing among the eligible items (X-179: As built (B1): 27 items printed by every surviving paper are admitted, and 8 more are chosen: the Paris report of the action of 21 May (5 of 6 papers, the French side of the campaign near Tournay), and for the kinds of news the admitted items leave out Congress's commercial resolutions, Britain's instructions of November 1793, the insurrection in western Pennsylvania, General Wayne's own letter and Mr. Jay's memorial: 33 stories in 36 groups. The other eligible items are not chosen and are listed with their counts.
for_user_decision.Filing and dates (X-1794-11): Data: the Gazette of the United States changes catalogue number on 12 June (C-04). The release's map of misfiled RevX pages lists 3 pages of 1794 (the Gazette of the United States of 22 July, pages 1 to 3), each holding the text of another page of the same issue; none holds a printing of the ledger.
for_user_decision.Headings above an item (X-1794-09): As built: an excerpt starts with the heading, dateline or date line printed directly above the item; a paper's own dateline over its column, the dateline of the paper an act or a letter was taken from, or a country heading over a run of foreign news stays out of the excerpt and is noted.
for_user_decision.Notices and titles of the items not chos: As built: eligible notices and advertisements are not chosen (C-10) and are described without the private persons they name (R-04); every other eligible item not chosen is listed by its own opening words, as the item finder found them.
for_user_decision.One affair's items (X-1794-03): As built (X-1800-01): the insurrection in the western counties of Pennsylvania is a parent story with three items: the President's proclamation of 25 September (4 papers), the Pittsburgh report of the meeting at Parkinson's Ferry (5) and the meeting's resolutions (5). The President's proclamation of 7 August is in 3 papers and listed below the bar.
for_user_decision.Printed again counts again (X-1794-04): As built (C-08): the Gazette of the United States printed the London paragraph on Jersey twice, the first of Mr. Madison's resolutions three times and the President's proclamation of 25 September three times; the Patowmac Guardian and the New Hampshire Gazette printed the paragraph on Jersey twice; each printing is in its group.
for_user_decision.Publications counted by their opening (X: As built (X-1810-01): the President's message of 21 May with the Secretary of State's letters to the British minister, General Wayne's letter with the War Office's introduction, and Mr. Jay's memorial with Lord Grenville's answer are each one item, counted by the opening of the main text.
for_user_decision.The London Gazette's formula (X-1794-02): As built (C-02): the Gazette's dispatches open with the same formula ('A letter, of which the following is an extract, was yesterday received from his Royal Highness the Duke of York, by the Right Hon. Henry Dundas'), so counts by opening reached each other's pages; each dispatch was counted at 60% of its opening's 5-grams, or by its letter's own words, and the pages were read.
for_user_decision.The papers in print and the bar (X-1794-: 9 catalogue series, 8 papers (the Gazette of the United States under two catalogue numbers, C-04); the Eagle (3 issues) and the Phoenix (1 issue) survive only in a few weeks, the Columbian Informer from February; 4 to 7 papers are in print in any three weeks, so an item needs 4 papers all year.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1794 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 1,022 items, 383 in 4 or more catalogue series by the finder's count), and the families of 1793 were looked for on the 1794 pages (items_from_1793.json: 78 items). Every item in 3 or more papers was counted by machine by about 100 words of its text from the finder's position, over all 2,119 pages in both transcriptions (a dense run of its word 5-grams, at least a quarter of them); the counts were joined into documents only where two items stand at the same place on the same pages, because the papers print runs of short foreign paragraphs. Every item the machine put in every surviving paper, and the news considered for choosing, was counted again by about 70 words from its own opening (counts_1794.json), and the pages that print another text sharing the words (the London Gazette's formula for its dispatches, the forms of the King's instructions) were read and left out. Each admitted printing was checked against its page scan.

value.paper_counting: 1794 has 9 catalogue series, which are 8 papers (C-04): the Gazette of the United States under two catalogue numbers (sn83025878 to 11 June, sn84026271 from 12 June). The Eagle of Hanover (3 issues) and the Phoenix of Dover (1 issue) survive only in a few weeks, and the Columbian Informer of Keene from February; 4 to 7 papers are in print in any three weeks, so an item needs 4 papers all year.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (register Y-THIN, chosen by the owner on 23 November 2026 and amended the same night with the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4; the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted (27 in 1794), and the others are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (a target, not a quota); one affair's items are handled as in X-1800-01; the eligible items not chosen are listed here.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Of 130 items eligible by the count, 3 are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks, counted by their own words, and are admitted: the King's speech at the opening of Parliament (7 of 7), the brig Lydia's news from Amsterdam (6 of 6) and Commodore Warren's dispatches from Quiberon Bay (4 of 4). 18 are chosen; the others are listed as not chosen, except five items on private persons, listed for the owner.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: The paragraph on the President's message on the Georgia lands, the sloop Delia's report and Commodore Warren's dispatches in a Philadelphia or London form and a New York form; the treaty with Prussia in two translations (C-02). The Patowmac Guardian's own paragraph on the French ships in the Chesapeake is another text and is not counted with the Baltimore letter.
counted_item_by_item.The acts by their own words: The automatic families join the acts of Congress and of New Hampshire by their formulas; counted by each act's opening, the naturalization act is in 5 papers and the others in 3 or fewer (below the bar).
counted_item_by_item.The treaty with Great Britain by its own: The treaty is in 4 papers by its own words: the Patowmac Guardian's printing of 18 July is 'concluded from our last', and its issue of 11 July does not survive (C-06); the Kentucky Gazette's essay of 3 October and the Gazette of the United States' commentaries quote its articles (C-07); the Gazette of the United States has no issue from 1 to 7 July.

for_user_decision.A transcription that garbles an opening: As built (X-1795-06): the Mirrour's printing of the President's proclamation, on a page torn at the top right, is counted: its opening survives in part, RevX garbles it, and the scan check reads it on the scan.
for_user_decision.Five items on private persons: Listed for the owner without names (X-1795-07).
for_user_decision.Grading calls on the transcriptions: The scan check graded the transcriptions by the protocol (C-14), as for 1774, 1775, 1783 and 1791. Calls the owner may revisit: (1) a word read as another real word that changes the sense is fact-changing, even where it is one or two words: 'encroaching' for the printed 'encreasing' (S95-005, S95-009), 'bail you with views' for 'hail you with vows' (S95-050), 'vicious' for 'riotous' (S95-082), and 'attended' for the misprint 'assended' (S95-074); (2) a name read as another name is fact-changing ('Robespierre' for Rewbel, S95-075; 'S. Willems' for S. Wiseleus, S95-052; 'Prins' for Pruys, S95-064, medium confidence), while a name a letter or two off is minor ('Pruyss', 'Thoem', 'P. J. B. F.'); (3) on the torn page of the Mirrour of 16 January, words lost to the tear are not counted, but RevX's 'concern' and 'confirmation' where the surviving letters read 'consola…' and 'contin…' are fact-changing (S95-006); (4) a misprinted year read as another year is fact-changing ('1775' for the printed '1725', S95-046), while a misprint RevX corrects silently is minor and recorded as a printed difference ('conrary', 'referance', 'Dispatchs'); (5) figures read on enlargements: the broken '20' that RevX reads '25' (S95-002) and the worn fraction '½' that it reads '3/4' (S95-098, medium confidence); (6) where RevX closes an item with '...' and the print goes on, the words are counted as dropped, fact-changing (S95-044).
for_user_decision.One paper under two numbers or titles: As built (X-1795-02): the Gazette of the United States under two catalogue numbers, and The Mirrour and The Federal Mirror of Concord, each counted as one paper (C-04).
for_user_decision.Printed forms counted together: As built (X-1795-03): the Georgia message, the sloop Delia, the treaty with Prussia and Commodore Warren's dispatches, each with its other form (C-02).
for_user_decision.The acts by their own words: As built (X-1795-05): each act counted by its own opening; only the naturalization act reaches the bar.
for_user_decision.The choice for 1795: As built (X-1795-01): 3 groups admitted by the rule's first part and 18 chosen, 21 stories and 102 printings; the other eligible items are listed as not chosen.
for_user_decision.The treaty with Great Britain: As built (X-1795-04): 4 papers by its own words, chosen; for the February news of the treaty the Western Posts (6 of 7) is chosen and Mr. Jay's letter to his brother (5 of 7) is not (X-1800-01).

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1795 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 481 items found on the pages, 145 in 4 or more papers by the finder's count), and again with the families of 1794 over the 1795 pages (items_from_1794.json: 65 items found, 16 in 4 or more). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page and counted again by its opening; a sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers found 446 runs, and the runs no finder item covers were read. Counted item by item (153 entries; the daily proceedings of Congress and of the state legislatures left out as digests), 130 items meet the bar (count_1795.md); where an item's family or run also holds other texts (the acts share their formulas), its papers were counted by its own words. The admitted and chosen items were counted again by their own words over all 1,668 pages in both transcriptions, and read on every page.

No 1795 issue has a corrected date; the release's map lists 5 misfiled RevX pages of 1795, none of them a page of this ledger.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN, as amended on 23 November 2026, the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; as in R-01, the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35); one affair's items as in X-1800-01; digests are not admitted; sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) as in every year. In 1795 4 to 8 papers survive for an item's weeks, so the bar is 4 or 5.

counted_item_by_item.Counted by their openings: The reading checked every eligible item's opening on each page it counts; this review read every printing of the chosen items again before cutting their excerpts, and their counts stand.
counted_item_by_item.One paper under two catalogue numbers: C-04: the Gazette of the United States is sn84026273 to 30 June and sn83025881 from 1 July ('Gazette of the United States, & Philadelphia Daily Advertiser'); it is counted as one paper.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Every finder item of 1796 in 3 or more papers (and of 1795 over the 1796 pages) was counted by its own opening over all 1,552 pages in both transcriptions and merged into text units: 46 of 160 units met the bar. Reading them, with the sweep's passages, gave 162 items: 47 eligible and 115 below the bar. One is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks and is admitted; 27 are chosen (28 stories, 28 groups, 115 printings); 18 eligible items are listed as not chosen and 1 for the owner.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms together: C-02: the Patowmac Guardian prints the elephant, Captain Atkinson's news and Captain Seward's in its own words; the Kentucky Gazette prints the Baron de Carondelet in its own words and the ratifications of the British treaty without the Charleston paper's words; the Federal Mirror prints the papers on a general peace under its own heading ('Prospect of Peace terminated. London, April 14. The following very IMPORTANT PAPERS, were yesterday communicated') and General Moreau's report as a letter dated 'AMIENS, Aug. 15.'
counted_item_by_item.Printed in parts: The Kentucky Gazette prints the ratifications of the British treaty in two issues (19 and 26 March); the treaty with Spain runs over pages 1 and 2 in three papers. Each printing counts once, by its opening.
counted_item_by_item.The bar: Y-THIN: more than half of the papers that survive for the item's weeks (a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and at least 4. 1796 has 6 papers: the Gazette of the United States (Philadelphia, daily, under two catalogue numbers), the New Hampshire Gazette and the Kentucky Gazette survive all year, the Federal Mirror to November, the Patowmac Guardian in 29 issues, and the Eagle, or, Dartmouth Centinel in six; 4 or 5 papers are in print in most weeks, 6 when an issue of the Eagle falls in them. The bar is 4.

for_user_decision.Choosing among the eligible items (X-179: As built: the eligible items are taken in order of their papers and first printing, and each is chosen unless an item of the same affair, as the reading names it, is already chosen within a month of it (X-1800-01). So the year keeps one story of the war in Europe every second or third month (the Rhine in February, Pichegru in May, Italy in July, General Moreau's report in October), one of the Algiers affair (the Sophia, 5 papers), and one of the Royalists in France (the Cher, 5 papers). No item is eligible in March, November or December.
for_user_decision.Data issues (X-1796-04): As built: the New Hampshire Gazette of 16 April (No. 2055) is filed twice, under 9 and 16 April, so its issue of 9 April does not survive; the ledger uses the 16 April keys, and the in-print counts treat the 9 April filing as a second copy. RevX reads the Patowmac Guardian of 14 April as 'TUESDAY' (a Thursday). The Gazette of the United States stands under two catalogue numbers (C-04). The Patowmac Guardian of 12 May has its RevX transcriptions shifted by one page (the text filed as page 2 is page 3's), which the release's map does not list; the Spain and England printing is on page 3 and its excerpt is cut from the CA text there. A filing correction can re-file that issue's RevX pages.
for_user_decision.Items printed in their own words (X-1796: As built (C-02): seven printings, one in each of seven stories, print the item in the paper's own words or without its lead (the elephant, Captain Atkinson, Captain Seward, the Baron de Carondelet, the ratifications, the papers on a general peace, General Moreau's letter); each is counted with the item and its excerpt starts where that paper's item starts. Without them, six of these stories would have 3 papers.
for_user_decision.Private persons (X-1796-03): As built (R-04): one eligible item turns on a private person (a carter's cruelty to his horse, New York, May, 4 of 6) and is listed for the owner without names; five more items that turn on private persons are below the bar and listed without names.
for_user_decision.The papers in print, the bar and the cho: As built: Y-THIN as amended (B1) with 6 papers (7 catalogue series, C-04); the bar of 4 makes 47 items eligible. One is printed by every paper in print and admitted (General Moreau's report, 5 of 5); 27 others are chosen (28 stories, 28 groups, 115 printings); 18 are listed as not chosen and 1 for the owner.

value.selection_rule: Adopted for 1797 on 23 November 2026, on the review's recommendation, which the owner asked it to follow: a story needs one single printed item in 4 or more papers, because only 8 series survive for 1797 (three all year, 2 to 6 in print in any three weeks), so no item reaches 7 papers, or 6; 1793 uses 6 for the same reason. Every single item in 5 papers was admitted, except digests; items in 4 papers were chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news: every document, letter or report in 4 papers was chosen, and single paragraphs of London, Paris and Hamburg news columns, verse, an anecdote and a printer's notice were not. Items are counted by their own words; a printing counts where its opening survives; two printed forms of one report are counted together, as 1809 counted two translations of one bulletin. A sub-story could have fewer papers under a parent that reaches the threshold; this round has none. The 21 stories of rounds one and two stay as they are; this round adds groups beside them.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1798 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 387 items, 83 in 4 or more papers by the finder's count), and the families of 1797 were looked for on the 1798 pages (items_from_1797.json). Every item the machine put in every surviving paper, and the news considered for choosing, was counted again by about 70 words from its own opening, the acts of Congress by their first section's own words (counts_1798.json), and every page found was read; the bills printed before the acts they became, in other words, are counted apart. value.paper_counting: 1798 has 8 catalogue series, which are 8 papers. The Gazette (Portland) survives from April, the Virginia Argus in 10 issues, the Wilmington Mercury in September and October and the Eagle of Hanover in 2 issues; 4 to 8 papers are in print in any three weeks, so an item needs 4 papers, and 5 in the weeks when all 8 are in print.
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (register Y-THIN, chosen by the owner on 23 November 2026 and amended the same night with the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4; the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted (4 in 1798), and the others are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (a target, not a quota); one affair's items are handled as in X-1800-01; the eligible items not chosen are listed here.

counted_item_by_item.A digest: 'Hamburg Summaries' (Lower Elbe, 22 June), printed by all four papers of its weeks, is a summary of the Vienna Court Gazettes and other news: a digest, not admitted (C-09).
counted_item_by_item.One report in two wordings, or abridged: Captain Freeman's news of the fleets (Boston, July: two wordings), the paragraph on the President's visit to Fort Independent (the Providence Journal in its own words), the report of the President's nomination of a minister to France (two wordings) and the Havana circular (under two introductions) are each counted as one item (C-02); the Portland Gazette prints the Trent paragraph of 7 May and the Roveredo paragraph without their first sentences, counted with them, as 1773 counted the Massachusetts Spy's paragraph on the Sheriffs' letter.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that are not printings: Pages that only quote an item are not counted (C-07): the Governor of Pennsylvania's message of March quoting the President's proclamation of 12 March; the address of the minority of the Virginia legislature, which quotes the Sedition Act and a Virginia law of 1785 (counted as one text, by its own opening); later paragraphs that quote the reports of the Secretaries.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: The 44 admitted and chosen items, the 89 eligible items not chosen, the 2 for the owner and the 25 read below the bar were counted by the first 40 words of their own openings against every page in both transcriptions, and the papers the comparison missed were looked for again and read; their papers are in counted_items.json.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs in runs of news: Foreign news reached the papers in runs of short paragraphs under London, Paris, Vienna, Hamburg and Italian datelines, which the Gazette of the United States, the New Hampshire Gazette, the Portland Gazette and the Providence Journal reprinted whole, in much the same order, in late July and August (C-09). Each paragraph is counted by its own opening: 32 of the 36 admitted items are single paragraphs or letters from such runs.
counted_item_by_item.Repeated printings and misfiled transcri: The Gazette of the United States prints the President's proclamation of 12 March in two issues; both printings are in the ledger. The Portland Gazette of 26 August has the RevX transcriptions of its pages 2 and 3 filed one page on (in the release's revx_page_map), so its ten printings on page 2 are cut from the CA text, as is the Providence Journal's page 3 of 27 February, whose RevX text lacks the item.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1799 that reach 3 or more papers, and those of 1798 over the 1799 pages, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 520 items, 515 printed somewhere, 137 reaching 4 papers by the finder's counts; items_from_1798.json: 387 items, 80 printed somewhere). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1799 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (393 texts, 114 at the bar by that count). For the texts one paper short of the bar (228) and those at the bar without every surviving paper (101), the missing papers were looked for again on their pages, by the text's words (the best page within its weeks) and by its names, and the strong candidates read. A sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers, over every page, found 1,483 clusters; the 82 passages that no finder item explains were read. The runs of foreign news that every surviving paper printed in July and August were counted paragraph by paragraph, each by its own opening (textcount.py), and the items at the bar were counted again by their openings read on their pages; printings on pages whose transcriptions are garbled or filed under another page were read by eye.

value.paper_counting: 1799 has 10 catalogue series, which are 9 papers: the Gazette of the United States, & Philadelphia Daily Advertiser (Philadelphia; a daily, 264 issues, to 20 December), the Providence Journal (52), the New Hampshire Gazette (Portsmouth; 52), the Portland Gazette under two numbers ('The Gazette', 16 issues to 22 April, and 'Jenks's Portland Gazette', 36 from 29 April: one paper), the Kentucky Gazette (Lexington; 19, to 9 May), the Mirror (Concord, N.H.; 11), the Republican Ledger (Portsmouth, N.H.; 11, from 19 September), the Virginia Argus (Richmond; 9) and the Eagle (Hanover, N.H.; 2). Papers in print in any three weeks: 5 to 8 from January to June; 4 from 9 July to 29 August (the Gazette of the United States, the New Hampshire Gazette, the Portland Gazette and the Providence Journal); 4 to 6 from September; fewer after 20 December, when the Gazette of the United States has no surviving issue. The bar is 4 papers in every week (5 for items first printed on 1 January).
value.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; digests are not admitted. Single paragraphs from runs of news are counted by their own words (C-09). In 1799 only four papers survive from July to the end of August, and they reprinted whole runs of foreign news, so 36 items are admitted by the rule's first part, most of them in July and August; 8 eligible items are chosen for the months and the kinds of news the admitted items do not reach (January to April, June, November, and the President's speech in December).

counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains the acts of the first session of the Sixth Congress through their enacting formula, signatures and titles (items of up to 91 printings), the Washington resolutions with the proclamations that recite them, and the paragraphs of one run of London news (Kleber, Canton, the Brest fleet, Munich). Each text was counted by its own words: no act reaches 7 papers (six papers printed the laws of the session; the Portland Gazette printed few federal acts); the President's proclamation on mourning is in 6 papers, the joint resolutions it recites in 7.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote or summarise an it: Not counted: the Republican Ledger of 29 January, which summarises the Consuls' proclamation of 12 November 1799 ('In one of the Paris Journals it is asserted that the Constitution of the third year has perished'); the New Hampshire Gazette of 30 December, which summarises the navy pension report; the National Intelligencer of 31 December, whose debate on the mausoleum bill quotes the monument resolution; the proclamation of 6 January, which recites the resolution for 22 February.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted item by item, five items of 1800 reach 9 papers: the Senate's address of 25 November, the President's reply to it, the House's address and the President's reply to it, and the Salem report of the ship Brutus (9 with the New Hampshire Gazette's other account of the same arrival, 8 in one wording). Eight reach 8: the convention for the evacuation of Holland, the letter from Constantinople on Kleber, the report of floods in China, Lord Whitworth's convention with Denmark, the President's speech of 22 November, the King's speech of 11 November, the convention with France (two translations) and the Mortefontaine entertainment (two forms). Twenty-two reach 7. Every other item is in 6 papers or fewer by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs of the proceedings: Mr. Livingston's resolutions of 3 February 1800 reached the papers inside their reports of the House's proceedings; each such paragraph is counted as an item by its own words, as 1806 counted Mr. Gregg's resolution, 1809 Mr. Giles's and the 1804 review the paragraphs of the daily proceedings (X-1804-04); the day's proceedings as a whole stay a digest. The House's resolutions on Mr. Randolph's letter (7) and the paragraph on the House's first sitting in Washington (7) are counted the same way and not chosen.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again: A paper that printed an item again counts each printing (C-08): the joint resolutions of 23 December 1799 were printed again among the laws and resolutions of the session by the Gazette of the United States (22 July), the Providence Journal (10 September), the Oracle (11 October) and the Kentucky Gazette (13 October); the Kentucky Gazette printed the Ratisbon report on 6 and 13 October.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: One item printed in different wordings counts as one (C-02): the convention with France in two translations (6 + 2 papers); Melas's letter in two translations; the King's speech with two introductions; the Salem report of the Brutus, where the New Hampshire Gazette prints another Salem account of the arrival in other words and goes on with the same paragraphs; the Mortefontaine report in two translations (not chosen). Two different reports of one event are not counted together when they share no text: the frigate Boston's arrival with the French corvette Berceau is in 6 papers in one report, and a seventh paper prints a different one.

Every item in 6 or more papers was read on its pages or checked for a seventh paper by machine (about 220 words of its text compared with every page of the year), and every item that might reach 7 was counted again by its own words with phrase searches over all 2,575 pages in both transcriptions, reading every hit.

value.paper_counting: The Gazette of the United States has two catalogue numbers in 1800 (sn83025881 to 7 May, sn84026272 from 1 July): one paper, counted once (C-04). The Ulster County Gazette of 4 January 1800 has seven scanned pages: pages 5 to 7 are a second copy of pages 1, 2 and 4 (C-05); no admitted printing stands on that issue.
value.selection_rule: The one admission rule (R-01), as for 1776, 1805, 1806, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single printed item in 9 or more newspapers is admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; items are counted one by one; a sub-story may have fewer papers when its parent reaches 7. No year-specific threshold: items of 1800 reach 7, 8 and 9 papers. In 1800, 6 to 10 papers are in print in any three weeks (7 for most of the year), so from February to July an item in 7 papers was printed by every paper that survives for its weeks; no item first printed in May or June reaches 7. Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed is chosen and the others are listed as not chosen, unless they are separate public acts (the President's speech and each house's address and his replies). Nothing is held back for its subject.

counted_item_by_item.A sweep for short items: The reuse families join printings that share long passages, and the finder takes its candidates from them, so short items printed in many papers can be missed. As in the 1803 review (X-1803-09), every page of 1801 was swept for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 7 or more papers, and every passage found was counted by its own words. The sweep found two of the admitted items (the consul's circular of 15 May announcing the war with Tripoli; the Boston paragraph on Mr. Appleton's arrival with the ratified convention) and several items listed as not chosen (the Senate's confirmation of Mr. Dexter; the President and the kine pox; the telegraph to the Vineyard).
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains items that papers printed together: General Augereau's note with the Frankfort report and other European news of January; the parts of the inaugural address with Mr. Jefferson's farewell to the Senate; the London news of August on Cairo, the attack on Boulogne and the rumour of peace; the Gibraltar news of November on Alexandria and the schooner Enterprize; the acts of the second session of the Sixth Congress through their enacting formula. Each text was counted by its own words. No act of that session reaches 7 papers by its own title followed by its enacting clause: the laws were printed in full by four papers at most (the National Intelligencer, the Oracle, Jenks's Portland Gazette and the Providence Journal); the act for the more convenient organization of the courts of the United States (the judiciary act of February 1801) is in 4.
counted_item_by_item.Letters and proceedings: The President's letter to Lieutenant Sterett and the lieutenant's answer are counted apart (8 and 7 papers): some papers print them together, others a week apart. The court martial's sentence on Captain Little and the Secretary of the Navy's letter approving it are printed together in all eight papers and are one item. The House committee's report of 19 February and Mr. Jefferson's answer are printed together in all seven papers and are one item. Paragraphs of the reports of the House's and the Senate's proceedings are counted by their own words (X-1800-08, X-1804-04); none of 1801 reaches 7.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote, summarise or reci: Not counted (C-07): the inaugural address quoted in essays and comments (National Intelligencer, 6 March; Alexandria Advertiser, 9 March; Republican Gazette, 2 April and 28 May; Providence Journal, 17 June; Republican Ledger, 23 June; New Hampshire Gazette, 21 July; Portland Gazette, 26 October; Oracle, 31 October and 28 November) and printed in part as 'the governing principles of his administration' (Rhode-Island Republican, 17 October); the President's reply to the New Haven remonstrance quoted in essays and satire (Oracle, 1 August; Alexandria Advertiser, 3 August; National Intelligencer, 24 and 31 August; Monitor, 8 August; Portland Gazette, 16 November; Oracle, 12 December); the French First Consul's 'State of the Republic' summarised by five papers; the decree of St. Domingo on duties summarised by four papers; the chief of staff's report on the armistice of Steyer quoted in another account by two papers; the census returns given as a table by two papers.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted item by item, one item of 1801 reaches 9 papers: the London account of 17 August of the second attack on the flotilla at Boulogne (9, with the Oracle's and the Portland Gazette's first sentences in other words and the Rhode-Island Republican's printing from the third sentence). Thirty-one items reach 7 or 8 papers: nineteen are chosen, ten are not, and two turn on private persons. Every other item is in 6 papers or fewer by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again counts again: A paper that printed an item twice has two printings (C-08): the Oracle printed the preliminary articles of peace in its extraordinary of Wednesday 2 December and again in its regular issue of 5 December.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: One item printed within different reports or in different translations counts as one (C-02): General Augereau's note within a Frankfort report in five papers and in other runs of news in two (7); General Moreau's report of Hohenlinden in three translations (2 + 4 + 1 = 7); Captain Baxter's journal under different introductions (7); Commodore Dale's letter in six papers and the same passage as a Boston paragraph in two (8); the London account of the attack on Boulogne with three first sentences (9); the preliminary articles of peace in the English text and in translations from the Moniteur and from French papers (8).
counted_item_by_item.This year's printings: A reviewed year's group holds only that year's printings (C-11). The President's message of 8 December 1801, with his letter to the President of the Senate, is in 6 papers in 1801 (most papers printed it later in December or in 1802); General Augereau's note of November 1800 and General Moreau's report of December 1800 are admitted by their printings of 1801.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1801 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 1,240 items printed somewhere; by the finder's count, with papers that have two catalogue numbers taken as one, 2 reach 9 papers, 8 reach 8 and 29 reach 7). The same script was run with year 1800 over the 1801 pages (items_from_1800.json: 154 items printed somewhere, none in more than 5 papers). Every item in 7 or more papers was read, and every item in 5 or 6 papers that a comparison of about 220 words of its text with every page put in more papers was checked. A sweep of the year for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 7 or more papers, as the 1803 review introduced (X-1803-09), found short items that the reuse families had not joined, and those were counted too. Every item that might reach 7 was counted again by its own words, in both transcriptions, and with phrase searches over all 2,372 pages of 1801, reading every hit.

value.paper_counting: 1801 has 14 catalogue series, which are 11 papers (C-04): the Portsmouth Oracle (sn83025544, The United States Oracle of the Day, to 10 October; sn83025545, the United States Oracle and Portsmouth Advertiser, from 17 October, by the same printers on the same day of the week); the Republican Ledger (sn84023378 to 17 November, number 13 of volume III; sn84023379, the Republican Ledger and Portsmouth Price Current, from 24 November, number 14); and the Wilmington Monitor (sn84020424, The Monitor & Wilmington Repository, total number 103 on 23 May; sn84038116, The Monitor, or Delaware Federalist, total numbers 120 and 146). The other eight papers have one catalogue number each: the Alexandria Advertiser and Commercial Intelligencer, the National Intelligencer, the New Hampshire Gazette, Jenks's Portland Gazette, the Providence Journal, the Virginia Argus (January and February only), Elijah Russell's Republican Gazette of Concord (24 issues) and the Rhode-Island Republican (from October). Every count takes each paper once.
value.selection_rule: The one admission rule (R-01), as for 1776, 1800, 1802, 1803, 1804, 1805, 1806, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single printed item in 9 or more newspapers is admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; items are counted one by one; a sub-story may have fewer papers when its parent reaches 7. No year-specific threshold: items of 1801 reach 7, 8 and 9 papers. 6 to 10 papers are in print in any three weeks: 8 or 9 in January and February, 7 from March to June (8 in May), 6 in early July, 8 or 9 from mid-July and 9 or 10 from late September; from March to June an item in 7 papers was printed by every paper that survives for its weeks, and no item first printed in June reaches 7. Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed is chosen and the others are listed as not chosen, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01). Two items in 6 papers stand as sub-stories under parents that reach 7 (C-01), at the owner's decision of 23 November 2026: the merchants of New Haven's remonstrance, beside the President's reply to it, and the Knoxville paragraph that the treaty with the Cherokees is broken up, beside the Nashville paragraph on the treaty. Nothing is held back for its subject.

counted_item_by_item.Items printed together: Where one paper printed several documents in one column, each is counted by its own words: the Consuls' proclamation to the inhabitants of St. Domingo (7) and General Leclerc's own short proclamation that precedes it in several papers (5); the French Senate's address (8) and the First Consul's reply printed with it; the President's letter to Paine and letters of his to Callender printed in the same column of the Portland Gazette.
counted_item_by_item.Laws printed by authority: The item finder chains the acts of the first session of the Seventh Congress through their enacting formula and the list of acts (items of up to 9 papers and 96 printings). Counted by its own title followed by its enacting clause, no act reaches 9 papers and three reach 7: the act fixing the military peace establishment (admitted), the act for the apportionment of Representatives and the act establishing a uniform rule of naturalization (not chosen). Five papers printed nearly every law (the National Intelligencer, Kentucky Gazette, New Hampshire Gazette, Rhode-Island Republican and Republican Ledger); the Oracle, the Portland Gazette, the Alexandria Advertiser and the Virginia Argus printed some. Pages that mention an act in the proceedings, or recite it in another act, are not counted.
counted_item_by_item.Lists of the yeas and nays: Lists of members' names in the votes of the House (the finder joins several votes of February to August into one item of 7 papers) are parts of the proceedings, not items.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: One item in two wordings or translations counts as one (C-02): the Consuls' proclamation to the inhabitants of St. Domingo (4 and 3 papers: 'you are all Frenchmen ... But an entire change has taken place', and 'ye are all Frenchmen, ye are all free ... But all is changed'), General Leclerc's proclamation of 8 June (6 and 3), the French Senate's address to the First Consul for life (5 and 3), the New York report of the fire of 2 November (5 and 2), and the New York report of the Algerine cruisers (7, and the Virginia Argus's Philadelphia form, which opens in other words and goes on in the same).
counted_item_by_item.Standing notices and advertisements: The Postmaster General's proposals for carrying the mails (6 papers, 54 printings in successive issues) and a commission of bankruptcy against a trader (a legal notice, 6 papers by the finder's count) are advertisements; neither reaches 7 papers.
counted_item_by_item.The President's letter to Thomas Paine: Counted by its opening: 8 papers. A page that prints the letter whole counts, even inside an essay or among other letters, and the Alexandria Advertiser (12 October) and the Portland Gazette (6 December) printed it a second time (C-08); pages that quote part of it do not count (C-07): the Rhode-Island Republican's essay 'Seventy-Five, No. VI' of 25 September quotes only its first sentence, and the Alexandria Advertiser (16 October) and the Oracle (20 November) quote it from its second sentence.
counted_item_by_item.The Treasury report of December 1801: The Secretary of the Treasury's report of 18 December 1801 on the finances was printed in parts in January 1802; the finder makes items of its paragraphs. By its opening it is in 7 papers on 1802 pages (the National Intelligencer printed it in December 1801). Later pages that quote its figures (the National Intelligencer and the Virginia Argus in August and September) are not counted. The page of the National Intelligencer filed under 29 November that opens with the same formula is the issue of 29 December 1802 and prints the next year's report.
counted_item_by_item.The committee's report on the public mon: The report of the House committee appointed 'to enquire and report whether monies drawn from the Treasury have been faithfully applied' (April 1802) is chained by the finder into items of 9 papers. By its opening it is in 6 papers (National Intelligencer, Alexandria Advertiser, Republican Ledger, Kentucky Gazette, Republican Gazette, Oracle); the Recorder and the Rhode-Island Republican printed extracts from its later parts, which are not counted (C-06); the Virginia Argus and the National Intelligencer's 'History of the last session' summarise it (C-07).
counted_item_by_item.Thomas Paine's letters to the citizens: The finder makes items of single paragraphs of Paine's letters (up to 10 papers). Each letter is counted by its opening (C-06): the first letter is in 9 papers (the American Republican Gazette's printing of 7 December has its opening in print and in the CA text; RevX leaves it out), the second in 8, the third in 6 and the fourth in 6. Pages that quote passages in commentary are not counted (C-07): the Recorder's comments of 1 and 8 December, and the Alexandria Advertiser's reprint of them; the Kentucky Gazette's quotation of the first letter's last paragraph on 30 November; the Recorder's 'Extract from Paine's second letter' of 15 December; the Portland Gazette's quotations of the second and third letters. The passage on a 'female literary correspondent' that the first letter quotes also stands in Paine's letter to George Washington of 1796, which the Alexandria Advertiser reprinted in November; it is not counted with the first letter.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1802 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running), were split into single printed items (items.json: 1,378 items printed somewhere; 85 in 7 or more papers by the finder's count, 16 in 9 or more). Because the Treasury report, the proclamations of December 1801 and the acts of the session sit in families that began in 1801, the same script was also run with year 1801 over the 1802 pages (items_from_1801.json: 171 items, 19 in 7 or more). The finder's counts are those of chains (it joins items printed together, and acts that share the enacting formula), so every item in 6 or more papers was read in this session (Claude, the session's own model; no second reader) and counted by its own words, and every item in 5 or more was checked by machine for further papers: about 220 words of its text were compared with every page of the year in both transcriptions, and every page that shared many of its word sequences was read. Each act of the session was counted by its own title followed by its enacting clause. Each chosen item and each candidate set aside was counted with phrase searches on all 2,968 pages of 1802 in both transcriptions (story_phrase_search.py, phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json); every hit was read.

value.paper_counting: Papers, not catalogue numbers, are counted (C-04): Jenks's Portland Gazette (sn83016063 to 20 September, sn83016072 from 27 September: Number 230 and 231 of Volume V), the Recorder of Richmond (sn84024678 to 27 October, sn84024679 from 3 November: the same printers, Pace and Callender) and E. The 14 catalogue series of 1802 are 11 papers.
value.selection_rule: As for 1776, 1800, 1804, 1805, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single item printed in 9 or more newspapers was admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers were chosen to cover the months from January to December and the main kinds of news (Europe and St. Domingo; ships, trade and the Barbary states; American public life and government). Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed was chosen and the others were not, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01); the Barbary items were trimmed as in 1804 and 1805. Every story alike (the owner's rule of 11 November 2026): no item was left out for its subject. Where several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story. A group count is a target, not a quota.

counted_item_by_item.A sweep for short items: The reuse families join printings that share long passages, and the finder takes its candidates from them, so short items printed in many papers can be missed. This review also swept every page of 1803 for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 7 or more papers, and counted every item it surfaced by its own words. It found Colonel Despard's speech, Mr. Gascoigne's letter, the National Intelligencer's paragraph on the treaty of cession and the convention for the occupation of Hanover among the admitted items, and several items in 7 or 8 papers that are listed as not chosen. The earlier reviews did not run such a sweep (a note for the audit).
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains the acts of the second session of the Seventh Congress (and of the first session of the Eighth) through their enacting formula and the list of acts, the Secretary of the Treasury's reports of December 1802 and October 1803 through their common opening, and paragraphs of the House's daily proceedings. Each text was counted by its own words. No act reaches 7 papers by its own title: the laws were printed by authority in the National Intelligencer, the New Hampshire Gazette, the Republican Ledger, the Kentucky Gazette and the Rhode-Island Republican (5 papers), and a few also in the Recorder or the Oracle (6). The act of 31 October to take possession of Louisiana is in 6 papers; the Senate's bill for it, printed a week earlier, in 7 (not chosen; as 1809 kept a Senate bill apart from its act).
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote, summarise or reci: Not counted (C-07): the House's resolution of 7 January quoted in an essay on the purchase of Louisiana (National Intelligencer, 3 October), in a review of the session (Oracle, 26 March) and in a satirical paragraph (Alexandria Advertiser, 24 February); the Senate's resolutions quoted in the same essay; the Spanish minister's letter quoted in an essay (Alexandria Advertiser, 24 March); the Boston report of Mr. Eaton's arrival from Tunis quoted in the National Intelligencer's answer to it and in the Kentucky Gazette; the British declaration of May summarised by the Berkeley and Jefferson Intelligencer and the Kentucky Gazette; the Spanish royal order on Louisiana summarised by the New Hampshire Gazette and the Republican Ledger; the President's circular letter to the governors paraphrased in the Governor of New Hampshire's speech; the act to take possession of Louisiana named in the House's proceedings.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted item by item, six items of 1803 reach 9 or 10 papers: the President's message of 22 December 1802 on the deposit at New Orleans (9, by its printings of 1803), the Spanish minister's letter of 10 March (9), the French chargé d'affaires' letter of 11 March (9), the Spanish minister's letter of 19 April (10), Mr. Gascoigne's letter of 8 March brought by the ship Mercury (10, within three New York reports) and the President's message of 17 October (9). Twenty-three items in 7 or 8 papers are chosen and twenty-one are not. Every other item is in 6 papers or fewer by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs of the proceedings: As in the 1800 and 1804 reviews (X-1800-08, X-1804-04), each paragraph of the reports of the House's and the Senate's proceedings is counted as an item by its own words; the day's proceedings as a whole stay a digest. Three such paragraphs reach the band: the House's resolution of 7 January (8, admitted), the Senate's resolutions on 80,000 militia (8, admitted) and Mr. Ross's resolutions (7), and in the House Mr. Rutledge's resolution on duties on arms imported for the militia (7). The others the finder put in 7 or more are in 6 or fewer by their own words.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again counts again: A paper that printed an item twice has two printings (C-08): the National Intelligencer printed the Senate's resolutions on 80,000 militia as moved and as adopted, the Spanish minister's letter of 10 March again on 30 March ('We, therefore, re-insert it'), Colonel Despard's speech in two accounts, and the treaty and both conventions again with the President's proclamation on 2 November.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: One item printed within different reports or in different translations counts as one (C-02): Mr. Gascoigne's letter within three New York reports of the ship Mercury's arrival (10 papers; the reports themselves share no other text), Colonel Despard's speech within three London accounts of his execution (8), the French note of 13 May and the convention for the occupation of Hanover in two translations each, the Rotterdam paragraph on the Louisiana expedition with the Kentucky Gazette's shorter form, the Dublin letter with the New Hampshire Gazette's printing from its second sentence, and Mr. Monroe's letter with the Oracle's own heading.
counted_item_by_item.This year's printings: A reviewed year's group holds only that year's printings (C-11). The President's message of 22 December 1802 is admitted by its nine printings of January 1803 (the National Intelligencer printed it in December 1802); the President's annual message of 15 December 1802 is in 6 papers in 1803 and the Secretary of the Treasury's report of December 1802 in 7, most of their printings being of December 1802.
