value.paper_counting: 1803 has 17 catalogue series, which are 12 papers (C-04): the Alexandria Advertiser and Commercial Intelligencer (sn84024011, to 16 September) and the Alexandria Daily Advertiser (sn84024012, from 19 September, continuing its numbering); the Kentucky Gazette (sn82014782 on 4 and 11 January, then sn84038147); the United States Oracle of Portsmouth (sn83025545, to 15 October) and the Oracle Post (sn84023351, from 25 October), its country edition, which continues its volume numbering; Jenks' Portland Gazette under three catalogue numbers (sn83016072, sn83021505, sn83016081). Each counts once. No 1803 issue has a corrected date.
value.selection_rule: The one admission rule (R-01), as for 1776, 1800, 1804, 1805, 1806, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single printed item in 9 or more newspapers is admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; items are counted one by one; a sub-story may have fewer papers when its parent reaches 7. No year-specific threshold: items of 1803 reach 7, 8, 9 and 10 papers. 10 to 12 papers are in print in any three weeks from January to April, 10 to mid-June, and 8 or 9 from late June to December, so from July an item in 9 papers was printed by every paper that survives for its weeks. Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed is chosen and the others are listed as not chosen, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01). Nothing is held back for its subject.

counted_item_by_item.General Moreau: The finder joins the Moreau items of the year. Counted by their own words: the letter attributed to him by Les Nouvelles à la Main (No. II) 7, the same newsletter's No. III 7, the London paragraph on his banishment 8, and his letter to the First Consul of 17 Ventose, printed during his trial, 5 (in two translations).
counted_item_by_item.Laws printed by authority: The item finder chains the acts of the first session of the Eighth Congress through their enacting formula and the list of acts (items of 7 to 9 papers and up to 94 printings). Counted by its own text, no act reaches 7 papers: the act erecting Louisiana into two territories, the act for duties on imports and tonnage in the ceded territories, the act supplementary on the election of a President and Vice-President, and the act to protect commerce and seamen against the Barbary powers are in 5 or 6 papers each. The list of the session's acts is a list.
counted_item_by_item.Standing notices printed in successive i: The Secretary of State's notice that the amendment has been ratified ran in successive issues of several papers (the National Intelligencer four times, the Virginia Argus, the Rhode-Island Republican and the Kentucky Gazette three times each, the Enquirer twice); each printing counts, as 1807 counted the proclamation calling Congress: 17 printings in 7 papers.
counted_item_by_item.The House's daily proceedings: From November 1804 most papers reprinted the House's daily proceedings in the same words, so the finder makes items of 7 to 11 papers out of single paragraphs of those reports (motions, votes, memorials referred). Each paragraph is counted by its own words as an item, as 1806 counted Mr. Gregg's resolution, 1809 Mr. Giles's and 1800 Mr. Livingston's; the day's proceedings as a whole are a digest. One paragraph reaches 9 papers and is admitted: Mr. Griswold's motion of 12 November for an inquiry into drawbacks of duties at New Orleans (the committee's report on it, in 3 more papers, only quotes it). The others are in 8 or fewer: the motion to present a sword to Captain Decatur (8 as moved; the resolution as passed, printed by authority, in 3), the House's vote on it (8), the committee's return from the President on it (8), Mr. Randolph's question on the articles against Judge Chase (7), a memorial of 237 American citizens in Louisiana (7).
counted_item_by_item.The articles of impeachment against Judg: The finder joins the committee's report of 26 March 1804 and its report of 30 November 1804 into items of 9 and 10 papers. They are two reports, the second made on a new reference and adopted by the House, so each is its own group under the Chase parent, as 1809 kept a Senate bill apart from the act: 6 papers each (the National Intelligencer and the Virginia Argus printed both; together they reach 10 papers).
counted_item_by_item.The coroner's jury's verdict: The papers report it in three forms: the verdict quoted ('That Aaron Burr, Esq. Vice President of the United States, was guilty of the murder of Alexander Hamilton'; NI, VA, OP, EN, RIR, BJ), a shorter New York Gazette paragraph ('brought in a verdict of MURDER by AARON BURR'; ADA, BJ, EN, JPG, NHG) and the Norfolk Gazette's own words. Counted together as the verdict, as 1805 counted the accounts of Chase's acquittal and 1807 the Burr verdict: 10 papers, 13 printings (the Berkeley and Jefferson Intelligencer printed two accounts, the Enquirer three). The quoted verdict alone is in 6 papers.

value.method: The automatic families first printed in 1808 that reach 4 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running), were split into single printed items (items.json: 125 items in 7 or more papers). Because several of the year's most printed documents sit in families that began in 1807, the same script was also run with year 1807 over the 1808 pages (items_from_1807.json: 54 items in 7 or more papers). value.selection_rule: As for 1776 and 1807: every single item printed in 9 or more newspapers was admitted, except digests of unrelated paragraphs and items that need framing. Items in 7 or 8 papers were chosen to cover the months and the main kinds of news. Stories are counted item by item; where one publication holds several documents, or several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story. A sub-story may have fewer than 7 papers when its parent story reaches 7 (the rule the owner agreed for 1776 round two). A paper that printed an item again later counts each printing. Kentucky Gazette pages filed under 1808 are 1806 issues and were not used.

counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: Several finder items of 9 or more papers join different texts that share words: Canning's instructions and the Secretary of State's letter that quotes their conditions; the Intelligencer's statement of 13 November, the Secretary's letter of 8 November and later commentary; Jackson's circular and his secretary's note of the same day; the proclamations of April and August and the act they recite. Each text was counted by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Laws printed by authority: The item finder chains the acts of 1809 through their enacting formula and through titles recited in other acts, proclamations and debates (items of 9 to 12 papers and up to 101 printings). Counted by its own first section, no act reaches 9: the act to enforce the embargo and the non-intercourse act are in 8 papers, the act of 28 June in 7; the appropriation, relief, land and military acts in 5 or 6. The Senate's bill of June 1809, printed in four papers a week before the act, is not counted: its later sections differ from the act.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote an item: Editorials, speeches, debate reports and later documents that quote or recite an item were not counted: for example the essay that quotes Erskine's note of 17 April in the National Intelligencer of 26 July and the Delaware Gazette of 29 July, the commentary of 28 November in the New Hampshire Gazette that repeats the Intelligencer's words of 16 August, and Macon's bill of December, which recites the title of the act of 28 June.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again: A paper that printed an item again counts each printing: the Virginia Argus reprinted Erskine's April notes on 18 August, the National Intelligencer printed the message of 29 November twice in one issue (pages 1 and 5), the Alexandria Daily Gazette printed it on 29 and 30 November, and the proclamation and circular of 9 August were printed again in December.
counted_item_by_item.The December documents: The documents sent to Congress with the message of 29 November hold about twenty letters, which every paper printed in the publication's order over one to four issues. They were grouped by the publication's four parts, each counted by its first document; each letter's own count is in the second reader's proposal (12 letters in 9 or 10 papers).

counted_item_by_item.A letter counted across the reports that: The letter from on board the Vixen is printed after the National Intelligencer's paragraph in eight papers and with remarks of its own in the Rhode-Island Republican: counted by the letter, 9 papers (X-1803-02); the paragraph alone is in 8 (X-1810-02).
counted_item_by_item.Bills and acts: The act of 1 May 1810 is counted where it is printed under its own title (7 papers); Macon's bill no. 2, printed in April as reported and as ordered to a third reading, is not counted with it (X-1803-10).
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains the bills and acts on commercial intercourse, the President's proclamations and the Treasury's circular through their shared wording (the fourth section of the act of 1 May is quoted in the proclamation of 2 November and in the circular), the acts of the session through their enacting formula, the reports of the House's proceedings, and the documents of each publication of diplomatic correspondence. Each text was counted by its own words; only the act of 1 May reaches 7 papers by its own title among the acts of the session.
counted_item_by_item.Letters printed together: A letter and the enclosures printed with it are one item, counted by the letter's opening (C-03): Mr. Pinkney's letter of September with his note of 25 August and Lord Wellesley's answer; General Armstrong's letter of 10 March with his letter of that day to the Duke of Cadore. A publication of separate letters is counted letter by letter (R-01): of the despatches received by the John Adams, two letters reach 9 papers and fifteen are in 7 or 8; of the correspondence on Mr. Jackson's recall, Lord Wellesley's answer reaches 9 and Mr. Pinkney's two letters 8 each (X-1810-01).
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote, summarise or reci: Not counted (C-07): the Delaware Gazette's summary of the committee of ways and means' letter on loans; comments on the King's speech that quote its passage on America (ALX, ENQ, April); the Portland Gazette's extract of the Treasury's report of December, which leaves out its opening (C-06); the Enquirer's and the Virginia Argus's paraphrases of the President's message of 3 January in February.
counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted item by item, eleven items of 1810 reach 9 or 10 papers and are admitted by the rule's first part: the President's proclamation of 2 November (10), the Treasury's circular of the same day (9), the President's message of 5 December (9), the Duke of Cadore's letter of 5 August (9), Mr. Pinkney's letter sending Lord Wellesley's answer on the decrees (9), Lord Wellesley's answer of 14 March on Mr. Jackson (9), General Armstrong's letter of 10 March with his letter to the Duke of Cadore (9) and his letter of 7 April (9), the letter from on board the Vixen (9), the Natchez report from Baton Rouge (9) and the letter from Washington, Mississippi Territory, of 30 October (9). 47 items reach 7 or 8 papers: 13 are chosen (Mr. Pinkney's letter of 2 January as a sub-story beside Lord Wellesley's answer), 33 are not chosen, and the National Intelligencer's paragraph on the Vixen is counted with the letter it introduces. Two sub-stories under West Florida are in 6 papers (C-01).
counted_item_by_item.Printed again counts again: The French minister's note of 14 February printed again in the government's translation in late May (ALX, VA, ENQ); the Duke of Cadore's letter of 5 August printed twice in the Rhode-Island American; the decree of Rambouillet and the Duke of Cadore's letter printed again in December, with the documents sent to Congress with the President's message (Enquirer, Norfolk Gazette); the declaration of West Florida printed again in December with other papers of the convention (C-08).
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: The French minister's note to General Armstrong of 14 February in three translations (4, 5 and 3 printings; 8 papers, C-02); the decree of Rambouillet as its own text or within a paragraph from the Bulletin des Lois (8 papers).
counted_item_by_item.The resolution on General Wilkinson: The House's resolution of March 1810 for a committee to inquire into General Wilkinson's conduct (6 papers) and the same resolution offered again in December by another member (5) are two items, counted apart; neither reaches 7.
counted_item_by_item.This year's printings: 1810 is the collection's last year: the President's message of 5 December and the Treasury's report of December are counted by their printings of December 1810; later printings are not in the collection. Items of 1809 printed again in 1810 are counted by their 1810 printings (C-11): the Secretary of State's letters to Mr. Jackson of November 1809 are in 4 papers in 1810.

value.paper_counting: 1810 has 11 catalogue series, which are 11 papers; no paper appears under two catalogue numbers. The Delaware Gazette runs to 6 June, the Constitutionalist of Exeter from 21 May, and the Martinsburgh Gazette has four issues (27 July to 30 November). No 1810 issue has a corrected date, and the release's map of misfiled RevX pages lists none for 1810.
value.selection_rule: The one admission rule (R-01), as for 1776, 1800, 1802, 1803, 1804, 1805, 1806, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single printed item in 9 or more newspapers is admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; items are counted one by one; a sub-story may have fewer papers when its parent reaches 7. No year-specific threshold: items of 1810 reach 7, 8, 9 and 10 papers. 9 or 10 papers are in print in any three weeks of the year (11 only in the weeks of the Martinsburgh Gazette's four issues), so an item in 9 papers was printed by every paper, or all but one, that survives for its weeks. Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed is chosen and the others are listed as not chosen, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01). Nothing is held back for its subject. 1810 is the collection's last year: only printings dated 1810 are counted.
